14593.q: Which queen knighted Francis Drake after his voyage around the world?
14593.e: Queen Elizabeth I of England honoured Drake on board his ship in 1581. His voyage had brought England a lot of fame and treasure.
14593.m: Francis Drake was knighted by Elizabeth I.

14594.q: How did Jeanne Baret, the first woman to go around the Earth, travel on the ship at the start?
14594.e: At that time women were not allowed on naval ships. So in 1766 the botanist Jeanne Baret disguised herself as a man.
14594.m: Jeanne Baret was the first woman to go around the Earth.

14595.q: Which Swiss man, together with Brian Jones, was the first to fly around the Earth nonstop in a balloon in 1999?
14595.e: In 1999, Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones flew around the world without landing in the balloon “Breitling Orbiter 3”. They took off from Château-d’Oex in the canton of Vaud.
14595.m: Bertrand Piccard flew around the world in a balloon in 1999.

14596.q: Which Swiss aeroplane flew around the Earth in 2015 and 2016 without any fuel at all?
14596.e: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar energy alone. Two Swiss pilots took turns at the controls.
14596.m: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the Earth on solar power alone.

14597.q: Which notorious cape at the southern tip of South America was first sailed around in 1616?
14597.e: The Dutchmen Schouten and Le Maire sailed around the cape in 1616 and named it after the town of Hoorn. The waters there are known for storms.
14597.m: Cape Horn is named after the Dutch town of Hoorn.

14598.q: Which British seafarer explored the Pacific on several voyages around the world in the 18th century?
14598.e: From 1768, James Cook made three great voyages to the Pacific. Among other things, he mapped New Zealand and the east coast of Australia.
14598.m: James Cook explored the Pacific on three great voyages.

14599.q: What happened to Magellan during the first voyage around the world?
a: He died on the way, in the Philippines
He returned to Spain as a hero
He became king of an island
He chose to stay in South America
14599.e: Magellan was killed in a fight in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano then led the Victoria back to Spain.
14599.m: Magellan did not live to see the end of his voyage around the world.

14600.q: In which region did the Maya live?
14600.e: The Maya lived in what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and parts of Honduras and El Salvador. An important area is the Yucatán Peninsula.
14600.m: The Maya lived in Central America.

14601.q: Which number did the Maya know long before the Europeans?
14601.e: The Maya used a sign for zero that looks like a shell. In Europe, zero only caught on much later.
14601.m: The Maya were calculating with zero early on.

14602.q: Which base number was the Maya number system built on?
14602.e: The Maya counted in a base-20 system, probably because of fingers and toes. A dot stood for 1 and a bar for 5.
14602.m: The Maya counted in a base-20 system.

14603.q: Which crop was the most important food of the Maya?
14603.e: Maize was the basis of their diet and also played an important role in myths. According to a Maya story, humans were created from maize.
14603.m: Maize was the most important food of the Maya.

14604.q: Which famous Maya city is on the Yucatán Peninsula and has the pyramid “El Castillo”?
14604.e: Chichén Itzá was an important Maya city. The step pyramid El Castillo, also called the Temple of Kukulcán, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
14604.m: The pyramid El Castillo stands in Chichén Itzá.

14605.q: Which large Maya city is in the rainforest of present-day Guatemala?
14605.e: In the Classic period, Tikal was one of the largest Maya cities. Its tall temple pyramids rise above the rainforest.
14605.m: Tikal is a large Maya city in Guatemala.

14606.q: What did the Maya have, unlike the Inca?
a: A road network in the Andes
14606.e: The Maya wrote with glyphs, signs for words and syllables. They carved texts in stone and wrote books known as codices.
14606.m: The Maya had their own writing made of glyphs.

14607.q: What did the Maya write their books on?
14607.e: The Maya made a kind of paper from the bark of fig trees. They folded it into books like a concertina.
14607.m: Maya books were made of bark paper.

14608.q: Why are there only a few Maya books left today?
a: Spanish missionaries had many of them burned
The Maya only wrote on stones
An earthquake destroyed all the libraries
The Maya burned them themselves as offerings
14608.e: In 1562 the monk Diego de Landa had many Maya writings burned because he thought they were heathen. As a result, a lot of knowledge was lost.
14608.m: Many Maya books were destroyed by Spanish missionaries.

14609.q: What happened to many large Maya cities in the lowlands around the year 900?
a: They were conquered by the Spanish
They became capitals of the Inca
They were buried by a volcano
14609.e: Many cities in the southern lowlands were abandoned between about 800 and 900. Possible reasons include droughts, wars and overused soils.
14609.m: Around 900, many Maya cities were abandoned.

a: Yes, millions of people are Maya
No, they died out during the conquest
Yes, but only a few dozen
14610.e: Maya culture did not disappear. Today millions of Maya live in Mexico and Guatemala and speak many different Mayan languages.
14610.m: The Maya still live in Central America today.

14611.q: Which drink did the Maya make early on from the beans of a plant?
14611.e: The Maya drank bitter cocoa, often mixed with spices. Later cocoa came to Europe and was developed into chocolate.

14612.q: What was the name of the Aztec capital?
14612.e: Tenochtitlan was on an island in Lake Texcoco. Long causeways connected the city to the shore.
14612.m: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztecs.

14613.q: Which present-day capital stands on the ruins of Tenochtitlan?
14613.e: After the conquest, the Spanish built their city right on top of Tenochtitlan. Remains of the Great Temple have been dug up in the middle of Mexico City.
14613.m: Mexico City stands where Tenochtitlan once was.

14614.q: Where was the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan?
a: On an island in a lake
In the middle of the desert
14614.e: Tenochtitlan was on an island in Lake Texcoco. Causeways and canals connected the city to the shore.
14614.m: Tenochtitlan was on an island in a lake.

14615.q: According to their legend, which sign showed the Aztecs where to found their city?
a: An eagle on a cactus with a snake
A jaguar under a maize field
A llama on a mountain top
14615.e: According to the founding legend, the Aztecs saw an eagle on a prickly pear cactus holding a snake. This picture can be seen on the flag of Mexico today.
14615.m: The eagle on the cactus is the sign from the founding legend of Tenochtitlan.

14616.q: Which Spanish conquistador conquered the Aztec empire?
14616.e: Hernán Cortés landed on the coast of Mexico in 1519. With the help of local allies, he conquered the Aztec capital.
14616.m: Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec empire.

14617.q: What was the name of the Aztec ruler when the Spanish arrived in 1519?
14617.e: Moctezuma II received Cortés in Tenochtitlan. He was later taken prisoner and died in 1520 in unexplained circumstances.
14617.m: Moctezuma II ruled the Aztecs when Cortés came.

14618.q: In which year did Tenochtitlan fall to the Spanish?
14618.e: After a long siege, Cortés and his allies captured the city in August 1521. That was the end of the Aztec empire.

14619.q: Besides weapons and allies, what contributed greatly to the Spanish victory over the Aztecs?
14619.e: The Spanish brought smallpox, against which the people in America had no defences. In 1520 a great many people in Tenochtitlan died of this disease.
14619.m: Diseases brought in from outside greatly weakened the Aztecs.

14620.q: Which people fought as allies of the Spanish against the Aztecs?
14620.e: The Tlaxcaltecs were enemies of the Aztecs. Thousands of them fought on Cortés’s side.
14620.m: Without local allies, Cortés could hardly have won.

14621.q: Which language did the Aztecs speak?
14621.e: Nahuatl is still spoken by over a million people in Mexico today. Words such as “avocado” and “coyote” also come from Nahuatl.

a: Artificial garden beds in the lake
14622.e: Chinampas were fields built up in the shallow water of the lake. The Aztecs grew maize, beans and vegetables on them.
14622.m: On chinampas, the Aztecs grew plants in the lake.

14623.q: Which god did the Aztecs worship as the “Feathered Serpent”?
14623.e: Quetzalcoatl was an important god in Central America. The Maya worshipped a similar god called Kukulcán.
14623.m: Quetzalcoatl is the Feathered Serpent of the Aztecs.

14624.q: In which European city is the famous feather headdress known as “Moctezuma’s Penacho”?
14624.e: The headdress made of quetzal feathers is kept in the Weltmuseum in Vienna. Mexico has long wanted it returned.
14624.m: Moctezuma’s feather headdress is in Vienna today.

14625.q: What was the name of the capital of the Inca empire?
14625.e: Cusco is in the highlands of present-day Peru. The Inca saw the city as the centre of their empire.
14625.m: Cusco was the capital of the Inca.

14626.q: In which mountain range was the Inca empire?
14626.e: The Inca empire stretched along the Andes in South America. It reached from what is now southern Colombia to Chile.
14626.m: The Inca empire was in the Andes.

14627.q: Which famous Inca city lies high on a mountain in Peru and became internationally known in 1911?
14627.e: The American Hiram Bingham made Machu Picchu world-famous in 1911. But local farmers already knew the place before that.

a: A knotted cord for recording numbers
A temple for the sun god
14628.e: With knots in coloured cords, the Inca recorded numbers, for example for taxes and stores. Specialists could “read” these cords.
14628.m: The Inca stored numbers with knotted cords.

14629.q: Which language did the Inca speak?
14629.e: Quechua was the official language of the Inca empire. Millions of people in the Andes still speak Quechua today.
14629.m: The language of the Inca is called Quechua.

14630.q: Which animals did the Inca use as pack animals and for wool?
14630.e: Llamas can carry loads over steep mountain paths. For fine wool, the Inca also kept alpacas.
14630.m: The Inca kept llamas as pack animals.

14631.q: Which important crop originally comes from the Andes and was grown by the Inca?
14631.e: The potato was grown in the Andes long before the Inca. It came to Europe via Spain and later became a staple food in Switzerland too.
14631.m: The potato comes from the Andes.

14632.q: Which Spaniard conquered the Inca empire?
14632.e: Francisco Pizarro came to the Inca empire in 1532 with only around 170 men. A civil war between two claimants to the throne had weakened the empire.
14632.m: Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca empire.

14633.q: What did the Spanish demand as ransom for the captured Inca ruler Atahualpa?
14633.e: Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532. Although the Inca filled a room with gold and silver, the Spanish had him executed in 1533.
14633.m: The Spanish wanted gold and silver from the Inca.

14634.q: Into how many large parts was the Inca empire divided?
14634.e: The Inca called their empire “Tawantinsuyu”, the land of four parts. The borders of the parts met in the capital, Cusco.
14634.m: The Inca empire was made up of four parts.

14635.q: How did the Inca carry messages quickly through their empire?
14635.e: The runners were called chasquis and waited at stations along the roads. That way messages could cover long distances in a short time.
14635.m: Inca runners carried messages through the empire in relays.

14636.q: Which way of building is typical of Inca buildings?
a: Houses made of bamboo and paper
14636.e: The Inca cut stones so precisely that they held together firmly without mortar. Many of these walls even survived earthquakes.
14636.m: Inca walls hold together without mortar.

14637.q: Which treaty divided the newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal in 1494?
14637.e: In the Treaty of Tordesillas, a line was drawn through the Atlantic. Lands to the west of it were to go to Spain, lands to the east to Portugal.
14637.m: In 1494, the Treaty of Tordesillas divided the world between Spain and Portugal.

14638.q: Why do people in Brazil speak Portuguese and not Spanish?
a: Because Brazil was a Portuguese colony
Because Portuguese was a native language
14638.e: The Portuguese Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, after which it became a colony of Portugal. Brazil only became independent in 1822.
14638.m: Brazil was a colony of Portugal.

14639.q: What were the Spanish conquerors in America called?
14639.e: The word comes from the Spanish “conquistador”, meaning “conqueror”. The conquistadors were mainly looking for gold, land and glory.
14639.m: Conquistadors were the Spanish conquerors of America.

14640.q: What did many Indigenous people in the Spanish colonies have to do for the settlers?
a: Do forced labour and pay dues
14640.e: Under the encomienda system, Spaniards were allowed to demand work and dues from the local people. This often led to harsh exploitation.
14640.m: Many Indigenous people had to work for Spanish settlers.

14641.q: What did the Spanish priest Bartolomé de las Casas fight for in the 16th century?
a: The rights of the native peoples
14641.e: Bartolomé de las Casas described the violence of the conquerors and criticised the exploitation. He demanded better protection for the Indigenous people.
14641.m: Bartolomé de las Casas fought for the rights of the native peoples.

14642.q: Where were millions of people from Africa taken by force in the transatlantic slave trade?
14642.e: From the 16th to the 19th century, around 12 million Africans were taken to America by force. They had to do forced labour, mainly on plantations and in mines.
14642.m: The slave trade took millions of people from Africa to America by force.

14643.q: Which plant came to Europe as a result of the colonisation of America?
14643.e: Peppers, pumpkins and peanuts also come from America. This exchange between the Old and New Worlds is called the “Columbian Exchange”.

14644.q: Which animal did the Europeans bring to America, where it did not exist at the time?
14644.e: The Spanish brought horses to America, because America’s prehistoric horses had died out thousands of years earlier. Later, horses became very important to many Indigenous peoples of North America.
14644.m: Horses only came to America with the Europeans.

14645.q: Which precious metal from the mountain of Potosí, in present-day Bolivia, made Spain rich?
14645.e: From 1545, huge amounts of silver were mined at Potosí. The Indigenous workers had to work in very harsh conditions.
14645.m: Silver from Potosí brought Spain great wealth.

14646.q: Which country founded its first permanent settlement in North America, Jamestown, in 1607?
14646.e: Jamestown was in the colony of Virginia. The first years were marked by hunger and disease.
14646.m: In 1607, Jamestown was the first permanent English settlement in North America.

14647.q: On which ship did the so-called Pilgrim Fathers come to North America in 1620?
14647.e: The Pilgrim Fathers were English Protestants who wanted to practise their faith freely. They founded the settlement of Plymouth.
14647.m: The Pilgrim Fathers came on the Mayflower in 1620.

14648.q: Which city was first called “New Amsterdam” as a Dutch settlement?
14648.e: The Dutch founded New Amsterdam on the island of Manhattan. In 1664 the English took over the city and called it New York.
14648.m: New York was first called New Amsterdam.

14649.q: Which town in North America was founded in 1710 by settlers from Switzerland and the Palatinate?
14649.e: Christoph von Graffenried from Bern founded New Bern in what is now North Carolina. The town still has a bear in its coat of arms today.
14649.m: New Bern in America was founded by a man from Bern.

14650.q: Roughly when did Martin Luther live?
14650.e: Martin Luther was born in 1483 and died in 1546. So he lived about 500 years ago, at the same time as Zwingli.
14650.m: Martin Luther lived about 500 years ago.

14651.q: In which present-day country did Martin Luther live and work?
14651.e: Luther was born in Eisleben in 1483 and worked mainly in Wittenberg. Both towns are in today’s Germany.
14651.m: Martin Luther lived in today’s Germany.

14652.q: Which experience made Luther become a monk in 1505?
14652.e: On 2 July 1505 Luther was caught in a fierce thunderstorm near Stotternheim and, terrified of dying, vowed to become a monk. Soon after, he entered a monastery in Erfurt.
14652.m: A thunderstorm made Luther go into a monastery.

14653.q: Where did Luther live as a monk from 1505?
14653.e: In 1505 Luther became a monk in the Augustinian monastery in Erfurt. There he lived with other monks by strict rules.
14653.m: Luther lived as a monk in a monastery.

14654.q: What was Martin Luther supposed to study, as his father wished?
14654.e: His father wanted Luther to become a lawyer and have a career. Luther began studying law in Erfurt in 1505 but soon gave it up and went into a monastery.
14654.m: Luther’s father wanted him to become a lawyer.

14655.q: Before which ruler did Luther have to answer for himself at the Diet of Worms in 1521?
14655.e: At the Diet of Worms in 1521, Luther was supposed to take back his writings before Emperor Charles V. He refused, because no one had proved him wrong using the Bible.
14655.m: At Worms in 1521 Luther refused to take back his views before Emperor Charles V.

14656.q: What did the imperial ban imposed on Luther after the Diet of Worms mean?
a: He was an outlaw and anyone could seize him
He had to pay a large fine
He could only preach in Wittenberg
He had to leave the empire for a year
14656.e: With the Edict of Worms, Luther was outlawed. No one was allowed to protect him, and his writings were to be banned.
14656.m: The imperial ban made Luther an outlaw.

14657.q: In which castle did Luther hide after the Diet of Worms?
14657.e: Luther’s prince had him “kidnapped” for show and taken to Wartburg Castle near Eisenach. There Luther lived under the name “Junker Jörg” (Squire George).
14657.m: At Wartburg Castle Luther was safe as “Junker Jörg”.

14658.q: Why was Luther “kidnapped” for show in 1521 and taken to Wartburg Castle?
a: A prince wanted to protect him this way
He was to be punished there
The Pope wanted to question him
14658.e: Elector Frederick the Wise of Saxony was Luther’s prince. He had him “kidnapped” for show so that no one could harm him after the Diet of Worms.
14658.m: A prince took Luther to Wartburg Castle to protect him.

14659.q: Which important work did Luther begin during his time at Wartburg Castle?
a: Translating the New Testament into German
14659.e: At Wartburg Castle Luther translated the New Testament from Greek into German in about eleven weeks. It was printed in 1522.
14659.m: At Wartburg Castle Luther translated the New Testament into German.

14660.q: Why was Luther’s translation of the Bible so important for ordinary people?
a: They could now read the Bible in their own language
They got the Bible for free
Only priests were allowed to read the Bible
14660.e: Before, the Bible in church was mostly in Latin, which only scholars understood. Luther wanted all Christians to be able to read the Bible for themselves.
14660.m: Thanks to Luther’s translation many people could read the Bible in German.

14661.q: Whom did Martin Luther marry in 1525?
14661.e: Katharina von Bora was a former nun who had escaped from her convent. The marriage showed that Luther rejected the rule that clergy must not marry.
14661.m: In 1525 Luther married the former nun Katharina von Bora.

14662.q: What did the Pope do to Martin Luther in 1521?
14662.e: On 3 January 1521 Pope Leo X excommunicated Luther. Luther had refused to take back his teachings.
14662.m: In 1521 the Pope expelled Luther from the Church.

14663.q: What did Luther do in December 1520 with the papal bull that threatened him with excommunication?
a: He sent it to the emperor
He hung it up in church
14663.e: In front of the Elster Gate in Wittenberg, Luther burned the bull together with books of Church law. With that, he openly broke with the Pope.
14663.m: In 1520 Luther burned the Pope’s bull in public.

14664.q: What was Luther’s attitude to the rebelling peasants in the Peasants’ War of 1525?
a: He fought alongside them as a soldier
14664.e: Luther first called on the peasants to keep the peace, but then wrote sharply against the uprising and took the side of the princes. Many peasants felt betrayed by him.
14664.m: In the Peasants’ War Luther turned against the rebelling peasants.

14665.q: Which well-known hymn did Martin Luther write?
a: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God
Holy God, We Praise Thy Name
14665.e: “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God” was written by Luther and became the best-known song of the Reformation. Luther encouraged the whole congregation to sing in church services.
14665.m: Luther wrote the hymn “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God”.

14666.q: In which town is Luther said to have published his 95 Theses in 1517?
14666.e: Luther taught at the University of Wittenberg. In 1517 he published his 95 Theses against the sale of indulgences there. This is seen as the start of the Reformation.
14666.m: The Reformation began in Wittenberg in 1517.

14667.q: In which year did Luther publish his 95 Theses?
14667.e: In 1517 Luther made his 95 Theses against indulgences known. This year is seen as the start of the Reformation.

14668.q: Which practice of the Church were the 95 Theses mainly aimed against?
14668.e: Luther criticised the Church for selling letters of indulgence. People believed they could buy their way out of punishment for their sins with them.
14668.m: The 95 Theses were aimed against the sale of indulgences.

14669.q: What were people promised when they bought a letter of indulgence?
a: Being let off punishment for sins
14669.e: An indulgence was supposed to shorten punishment for sins, including in purgatory. For money you could even buy indulgences for people who had died.
14669.m: A letter of indulgence was supposed to cancel punishment for sins.

14670.q: Which Dominican monk preached for indulgences near Wittenberg and so angered Luther?
14670.e: Johann Tetzel sold letters of indulgence for the Church with great business sense. Many people from Wittenberg travelled to him to buy indulgences.
14670.m: Johann Tetzel was a well-known preacher of indulgences.

14671.q: Which saying is linked to the sale of indulgences in Tetzel’s time?
a: As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs
One God, one faith, one baptism
14671.e: The saying is attributed to the indulgence preacher Tetzel, but it is not proven that he really said it like that. It sums up what many people believed about indulgences, and that is exactly what Luther criticised.
14671.m: The saying about the coin ringing in the coffer shows how indulgences were sold.

14672.q: What was part of the money from the sale of indulgences at that time used for?
a: Rebuilding St Peter’s Basilica in Rome
14672.e: Half of the money from this indulgence was meant for rebuilding St Peter’s. The other half went to a German archbishop, who used it to pay debts to the banker Jakob Fugger.
14672.m: Indulgence money helped pay for St Peter’s in Rome, among other things.

14673.q: In which language did Luther write his 95 Theses?
14673.e: Latin was then the language of the Church and the universities. Only translations into German made the Theses known among ordinary people.
14673.m: Luther wrote the 95 Theses in Latin.

14674.q: What was Martin Luther when he wrote the 95 Theses in 1517?
a: A monk and professor of theology
A knight at the emperor’s court
14674.e: Luther was an Augustinian monk and taught at the University of Wittenberg. As a professor he was allowed to invite people to a scholarly debate.
14674.m: Luther was a monk and professor in Wittenberg.

14675.q: According to tradition, on which church door did Luther nail the 95 Theses?
a: The door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg
The door of St Peter’s Basilica
14675.e: Tradition tells of the Theses being posted on the Castle Church in Wittenberg. At that time this door served as a kind of notice board for the university.
14675.m: According to tradition, Luther posted the Theses on the Castle Church in Wittenberg.

14676.q: What do historians say today about the famous posting of the Theses with a hammer?
a: It is uncertain whether it really happened like that
14676.e: Luther himself never mentioned posting them. Only years later did Melanchthon and Luther’s assistant Georg Rörer report it, so the posting of the Theses is still disputed today.
14676.m: Whether Luther really posted the Theses is disputed.

14677.q: Which invention helped the 95 Theses spread widely within a few weeks?
14677.e: Thanks to Gutenberg’s printing press, the Theses could be reprinted quickly and cheaply. So they were soon being read in many regions.
14677.m: Printing spread the ideas of the Reformation very quickly.

14678.q: Which holiday recalls the publication of the 95 Theses?
14678.e: Protestant Christians celebrate Reformation Day on 31 October. In some German states it is a public holiday.
14678.m: Reformation Day is celebrated on 31 October.

14679.q: What did Luther originally want to achieve with his 95 Theses?
a: A debate among scholars about indulgences
The founding of a new church
14679.e: Luther wanted to improve the Church and invited people to a scholarly debate. At first, splitting the Church was not his aim.
14679.m: At first Luther only wanted to improve the Church, not split it.

14680.q: What is a “thesis” in the sense of Luther’s 95 Theses?
a: A statement that can be debated
14680.e: Theses are statements that are defended or disproved in a debate. Luther put forward 95 such statements.
14680.m: A thesis is a statement people can argue about.

14681.q: What did the excommunication imposed on Luther by the Pope in 1521 mean?
a: Luther was expelled from the Church
Luther had to move to Rome
Luther could only write in Latin
14681.e: Because Luther did not take back his teaching, the Pope expelled him from the Church. Shortly afterwards the emperor also declared him an outlaw.
14681.m: In 1521 Luther was expelled from the Church.

14682.q: According to Luther’s Theses, what is more important for a Christian than a bought indulgence?
14682.e: In the very first thesis Luther says that the whole life of believers should be one of repentance. In his view, anyone who truly repents does not need a letter of indulgence.
14682.m: For Luther, true regret counted for more than a bought indulgence.

14683.q: What does the Latin word “reformation” mean?
14683.e: “Reformatio” means restoration or renewal. The reformers wanted to renew the Church following the example of the Bible.

14684.q: What does the principle “sola scriptura” mean?
a: Holy Scripture alone is the measure of faith
14684.e: For the reformers the Bible was the only basis of faith. Church traditions only counted if they agreed with the Bible.
14684.m: “Sola scriptura” means that only the Bible counts.

14685.q: According to Luther’s teaching, how is a person made right before God?
a: By faith and God’s grace alone
14685.e: Luther taught “sola fide” and “sola gratia”: God gives salvation out of grace, and people accept it in faith. Good works follow from faith but buy nothing.
14685.m: According to Luther, people are made right by faith and grace alone.

14686.q: Where does the name “Protestants” come from?
a: From the protest of Protestant princes at the Diet of Speyer in 1529
From the name of a pope
14686.e: In 1529 Protestant princes and towns in Speyer protested against a decision of the Catholic majority. Since then the followers of the Reformation have also been called Protestants.
14686.m: The name Protestants goes back to the protest at Speyer in 1529.

14687.q: Which peace settlement in 1555 allowed the princes in the empire to decide the faith of their land?
14687.e: In the Peace of Augsburg, Lutherans and Catholics in the empire were legally recognised. The Reformed were not yet clearly included in it.
14687.m: The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 let the princes decide on religion.

14688.q: What does the principle “cuius regio, eius religio” mean?
a: The Church stands above the king
14688.e: The phrase was only coined by a lawyer around 1600, but it describes the arrangement of 1555. Anyone who did not want to accept their ruler’s faith was allowed to emigrate.
14688.m: “Cuius regio, eius religio” means that the ruler decides the religion.

14689.q: What is the reform movement of the Catholic Church in response to the Reformation called?
14689.e: The Catholic Church responded with inner reforms and tried to win back lost areas. A great council and new religious orders helped with this.
14689.m: The Catholic response to the Reformation is called the Counter-Reformation.

14690.q: Which council of the Catholic Church met from 1545 to 1563 to respond to the Reformation?
14690.e: The Council of Trent clearly set out Catholic teaching and got rid of abuses. With breaks, it lasted almost 20 years.
14690.m: The Council of Trent was the Catholic Church’s great answer to the Reformation.

14691.q: Which religious order was confirmed by the Pope in 1540 and became an important force of the Counter-Reformation?
14691.e: Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, which was confirmed in 1540. The Jesuits worked mainly in schools and in missions.
14691.m: The Jesuits were an important force of the Counter-Reformation.

14692.q: Which forerunner of the Reformation was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415?
14692.e: The Czech theologian Jan Hus criticised the Church much as Luther did later. Despite being promised safe conduct, he was burned in Constance in 1415.
14692.m: Jan Hus was a forerunner of the Reformation and died in Constance in 1415.

14694.q: Which sacraments remained in most Protestant churches?
a: Confession and anointing of the sick
14694.e: The Catholic Church has seven sacraments. The reformers kept only those they saw as set up directly by Jesus in the Bible.
14694.m: Protestant churches usually have only baptism and Communion as sacraments.

14695.q: What happened to many monasteries in areas that brought in the Reformation?
a: They were given to the Pope
14695.e: The reformers rejected life in a monastery as a way to salvation. The property often went to the authorities and was used, for example, for schools and care of the poor.
14695.m: In Reformed areas many monasteries were closed down.

14696.q: What did the peasants fight for in the Peasants’ War of 1525?
a: For more rights and lower dues
For a war against the Turks
14696.e: The peasants had to give their lords many dues and services. They demanded more freedom but were bloodily defeated in 1525.
14696.m: In the Peasants’ War the peasants fought for more rights.

14697.q: Which group in the Reformation period rejected infant baptism and only baptised adults?
14697.e: The Anabaptists believed that only people who consciously believe should be baptised. They were persecuted by Catholics and Reformed alike.
14697.m: The Anabaptists only baptised people who could believe for themselves.

14698.q: Which two reformers met in Marburg in 1529 for talks?
14698.e: Landgrave Philip of Hesse invited Luther and Zwingli to Marburg. They wanted to unite the Protestants, but did not fully succeed.
14698.m: Luther and Zwingli met in Marburg in 1529.

14699.q: On which question could Luther and Zwingli not agree in Marburg?
14699.e: Luther believed Christ was really present in the bread and wine. Zwingli saw it differently, so agreement failed on this point.
14699.m: Luther and Zwingli argued about Holy Communion.

14700.q: In which city did Huldrych Zwingli bring in the Reformation?
14700.e: Zwingli came from Wildhaus in the Toggenburg. As a priest in Zurich he began to renew the Church from 1519.
14700.m: Zwingli brought the Reformation to Zurich.

14701.q: In which church in Zurich did Zwingli preach?
14701.e: Zwingli took up his post at the Grossmünster in 1519. The Reformation in Zurich began from here.
14701.m: Zwingli preached at the Grossmünster in Zurich.

14702.q: What is the renewal of the Church that Zwingli led in Zurich called?
14702.e: Zwingli and his helpers wanted to renew the Church according to the Bible. This movement is called the Reformation.
14702.m: Zwingli was a reformer in Zurich.

14703.q: What was Zwingli’s job before he became a reformer?
14703.e: Zwingli was first a Catholic priest in Glarus and Einsiedeln. Only in Zurich did he begin to reform the Church.
14703.m: Zwingli was first a Catholic priest.

14704.q: What happened at the famous “sausage eating” in Zurich in 1522?
a: People ate sausage during Lent on purpose
The Bishop of Constance was honoured
14704.e: Sausage was eaten during Lent in the house of a Zurich printer. Zwingli was there but did not eat any himself; afterwards, though, he defended breaking the fast using the Bible.
14704.m: The sausage eating of 1522 was a public break with the fasting rules.

14705.q: Which invention helped Zwingli to spread his ideas quickly?
14705.e: Zurich printers like Christoph Froschauer printed Zwingli’s writings and the Zurich Bible. That way his ideas reached many people.
14705.m: Printing spread the ideas of the Reformation.

14706.q: What happened at the First Zurich Disputation in January 1523?
a: The council allowed Zwingli to keep preaching from the Bible
14706.e: On 29 January 1523 Zwingli defended his teaching in front of about 600 people. Afterwards the Zurich council decided that he could go on preaching, which opened the way to the Reformation.
14706.m: After the First Zurich Disputation in 1523 Zwingli was allowed to keep preaching.

14707.q: What was the most important guide for faith for Zwingli?
14707.e: Zwingli only wanted to accept what is written in the Bible. That is why he preached straight from the Bible.
14707.m: For Zwingli the Bible counted most.

14708.q: What was removed from the churches in Zurich from 1524?
14708.e: Zwingli rejected the worship of images as idolatry. In 1524 pictures, statues and altars were removed from the churches in an orderly way.
14708.m: In Zurich the pictures were removed from the churches in 1524.

14709.q: What did Zwingli do publicly in 1524 that Catholic priests were not allowed to do?
14709.e: Catholic priests were not allowed to marry. In 1524 Zwingli publicly married the widow Anna Reinhart and so openly broke this rule.
14709.m: Zwingli married as a priest and so broke with celibacy.

14710.q: Which Swiss practice did Zwingli fight against in particular, because he had seen it as an army chaplain?
a: Going off to fight as a mercenary
14710.e: Zwingli went with troops from Glarus as an army chaplain, including to the Battle of Marignano in 1515. After that he sharply criticised mercenary service and the payments from foreign princes.
14710.m: Zwingli fought against the Confederates serving as mercenaries.

14711.q: How did Huldrych Zwingli die in 1531?
a: He fell in the Battle of Kappel
He died of plague in Zurich
14711.e: In the Second War of Kappel, Zwingli marched with the Zurich troops against the Catholic cantons. He fell on 11 October 1531 at Kappel am Albis.
14711.m: Zwingli fell in the Battle of Kappel in 1531.

14712.q: Who became Zwingli’s successor at the Grossmünster after his death in 1531?
14712.e: Heinrich Bullinger led the Zurich church for over 40 years. He strengthened the Reformation and was in contact with Protestants all over Europe.
14712.m: Heinrich Bullinger became Zwingli’s successor in Zurich.

14713.q: How did Zwingli understand Holy Communion?
a: As a meal of remembrance in which bread and wine stand for Christ
As a sacrifice offered by the priest
As a feast only for priests
14713.e: For Zwingli, Communion was a meal of remembrance for the congregation. He understood the words “this is my body” as “this means my body”.
14713.m: For Zwingli, Communion was a meal of remembrance.

14714.q: Which translation of the Bible was made in Zurich in Zwingli’s time?
14714.e: Zwingli and other scholars translated the Bible into German in Zurich. The complete Zurich Bible was published in 1531.
14714.m: The Zurich Bible was made in Zurich.

14715.q: Which meal in the First War of Kappel in 1529 became a symbol of reconciliation among the Confederates?
14715.e: According to tradition, soldiers from both sides ate milk soup with bread together from one pot. The war ended in 1529 without a big battle.
14715.m: The Kappel milk soup stands for reconciliation among the Confederates.

14716.q: In which country was John Calvin born?
14716.e: Calvin came from Noyon in northern France. Because Protestants were persecuted, he had to leave France.

14717.q: Was Calvin older or younger than Luther and Zwingli?
14717.e: Calvin was born in 1509, Luther in 1483 and Zwingli in 1484. So he belonged to the second generation of reformers.
14717.m: Calvin was younger than Luther and Zwingli.

14718.q: In which Swiss city did Calvin work for most of his life?
14718.e: Calvin came to Geneva in 1536 and shaped the city until his death. As a result Geneva became a centre of the Reformation.

14719.q: How did Calvin explain the Reformed faith in detail?
14719.e: Calvin’s main work, the “Institutes”, was published in Basel in 1536. He revised and expanded it several times.
14719.m: Calvin explained the faith in a big textbook.

14720.q: Why did Calvin have to flee from France?
a: He was looking for work in a factory
14720.e: In France followers of the Reformation were persecuted. So Calvin fled and came to Geneva in 1536.
14720.m: Calvin fled France as a Protestant.

14721.q: What role did Calvin have in Geneva?
a: He was a pastor and preacher
14721.e: Calvin preached in Geneva and led the Reformed church. He held no political office, yet he still shaped the city strongly.
14721.m: Calvin was a pastor in Geneva.

14724.q: How was life in Geneva regulated under Calvin’s influence?
a: With strict rules on behaviour and church attendance
By the laws of the Pope
By the orders of the emperor
14724.e: Calvin’s church order of 1541 created the Consistory, which watched over the lives of the citizens. Dancing, gambling and luxury were strictly limited.
14724.m: In Calvin’s Geneva strict rules applied to daily life.

14725.q: How were people treated in Calvin’s Geneva who held a different religious teaching?
a: They were punished harshly, one even with death
They were allowed to preach freely
14725.e: In 1553 the Geneva council had the scholar Michael Servetus burned because of his teaching. Calvin had spoken against him. This is a dark chapter of the Reformation.
14725.m: People of other beliefs were persecuted in Calvin’s Geneva too.

14727.q: What did Calvin wish for his grave?
a: A simple grave with no special marking
A place in St Peter’s Basilica
14727.e: Calvin died in Geneva in 1564. He did not want to be worshipped, so his grave was not specially marked.

14728.q: Which nickname did Geneva get because of Calvin?
14728.e: Under Calvin, Geneva became the most important centre of the Reformed. That is why the city was called the “Protestant Rome”.
14728.m: Geneva was called the Protestant Rome.

14729.q: What were the French followers of Calvinism called?
14729.e: The Huguenots were persecuted in France for a long time. Many fled to Reformed areas, including Geneva and other parts of Switzerland.
14729.m: The French Calvinists were called Huguenots.

14730.q: Which monument in Geneva shows Calvin together with Farel, Beza and Knox?
a: The Reformation Wall in the Parc des Bastions
14730.e: Work on the Reformation Wall began in 1909 for Calvin’s 400th birthday. It shows the four reformers as large stone figures.
14730.m: The Reformation Wall in Geneva honours Calvin and other reformers.

14731.q: Where did Calvin’s teaching spread to?
a: To France, the Netherlands and Scotland
14731.e: Calvin’s students took his teaching to many countries. In Scotland John Knox founded the Presbyterian Church.
14731.m: Calvin’s teaching spread to many countries in Europe.

14732.q: Which two Swiss cities were the most important centres of the Reformed?
14732.e: Zwingli and Bullinger worked in Zurich, Calvin in Geneva. In 1549 the two cities agreed in their beliefs about Holy Communion.
14732.m: Zurich and Geneva were centres of the Reformation.

14733.q: Which large canton of the Confederation also became Reformed in 1528, after Zurich?
14733.e: After the Bern Disputation in January 1528, the council decided on the Reformation for the whole Bernese territory. Bern was then the largest and most powerful member of the Confederation.

14734.q: Which Swiss city on the Rhine accepted the Reformation in 1529?
14734.e: After unrest and an outbreak of image-breaking, the Reformation was introduced in Basel in 1529. The preacher Johannes Oecolampadius had long worked for it.

14735.q: What did followers of the Reformation destroy in Basel in 1529 in an outbreak of image-breaking?
a: Pictures and statues in the churches
All the books in the city
14735.e: The Reformed felt that pictures of saints did not belong in church. In February 1529 they tore many of them out in Basel.
14735.m: In the image-breaking, pictures and statues were removed from churches.

14736.q: Which town became Reformed even though a large Catholic monastery remained in its middle?
14736.e: The town of St Gallen became Reformed under mayor Vadian. But the abbey with its famous library remained Catholic.
14736.m: In St Gallen a Reformed town and a Catholic abbey stood side by side.

14737.q: Which cantons of Central Switzerland stayed Catholic during the Reformation?
a: Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne and Zug
14737.e: The five inner cantons held on to the old faith. They faced the Reformed cities in the Wars of Kappel.
14737.m: The five cantons of Central Switzerland stayed Catholic.

14738.q: Which city canton, besides Fribourg, stayed Catholic even though it was a city?
14738.e: Among the city cantons, Fribourg and Solothurn kept the old faith. Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen became Reformed.
14738.m: Fribourg and Solothurn stayed Catholic as cities.

a: Bern brought in the Reformation after conquering it in 1536
Vaud was reformed by the Pope
14739.e: In 1536 Bern conquered Vaud from Savoy. After that, Bern imposed the Reformation there.
14739.m: Vaud became Reformed after it was conquered by Bern.

14740.q: Which place in western Switzerland accepted the Reformation around 1530 with Bern’s support?
14740.e: The preacher Guillaume Farel preached in western Switzerland on Bern’s behalf. In 1530 Neuchâtel accepted the Reformation.

14741.q: How did the Second War of Kappel in 1531 end?
a: With a victory for the Catholic cantons
With the break-up of the Confederation
14741.e: The Catholic cantons defeated the people of Zurich on 11 October 1531 at Kappel am Albis. After that the Reformation could not spread further across the whole Confederation.
14741.m: The Catholic cantons won the Second War of Kappel in 1531.

14742.q: What did the Second Peace of Kappel of 1531 settle?
a: Each canton could keep its own faith
All cantons had to become Reformed
All cantons had to become Catholic
14742.e: The peace recognised that the Confederation was split into different faiths. In the jointly ruled territories the Catholic faith was favoured.
14742.m: After 1531 the Confederation stayed divided by faith.

14743.q: How did the authorities in Zurich treat the Anabaptists?
a: They persecuted them and executed some
14743.e: The Anabaptists rejected infant baptism and were persecuted for it. In 1527 Felix Manz became the first Anabaptist in Zurich to be drowned in the Limmat.
14743.m: The Anabaptists were persecuted in Zurich.

14744.q: Who carried on the Reformation in Zurich after Zwingli’s death in 1531?
14744.e: Heinrich Bullinger led the Zurich church for over 40 years. He also wrote a confession of faith that many Reformed churches adopted.
14744.m: Heinrich Bullinger was Zwingli’s successor in Zurich.

14745.q: Which canton split into two half-cantons in 1597 for religious reasons?
14745.e: Appenzell split into Catholic Innerrhoden and Reformed Ausserrhoden. Basel only split in 1833, and for other reasons.
14745.m: In 1597 Appenzell split into Innerrhoden and Ausserrhoden.

14746.q: In which canton did Catholics and Reformed live side by side after the Reformation, sometimes sharing churches?
14746.e: In Glarus both faiths existed after the Reformation. In some municipalities Catholics and Reformed used the same church.
14746.m: In the canton of Glarus both faiths lived side by side.

14747.q: Which wars between Catholic and Reformed cantons took place in 1656 and 1712?
14747.e: Both Villmergen Wars were decided near Villmergen in Aargau. In 1656 the Catholics won, in 1712 the Reformed.
14747.m: The Villmergen Wars were wars of religion in the Confederation.

14748.q: Which city in Vaud became Reformed in 1536 after Bern had conquered the area?
14748.e: After conquering Vaud, Bern imposed the Reformation there. Afterwards Pierre Viret preached in Lausanne.

14749.q: Which of these is one of the Swiss towns that introduced the Reformation in 1529?
14749.e: Schaffhausen accepted the Reformation in 1529 after hesitating for a long time. Lucerne, Fribourg and Zug stayed Catholic.

14750.q: What nickname does the French king Louis XIV have?
14750.e: Louis XIV chose the sun as his symbol. Just as the sun stands at the centre, the king was to stand at the centre of the state.
14750.m: Louis XIV is called the “Sun King”.

14751.q: Roughly how long was Louis XIV King of France?
14751.e: Louis XIV became king in 1643 and died in 1715. With about 72 years, he had one of the longest reigns in European history.

14752.q: How old was Louis XIV when he became king in 1643?
14752.e: Louis XIV was born in 1638. When his father Louis XIII died in 1643, he was only four years old.
14752.m: Louis XIV became king when he was a small child.

14753.q: Which famous sentence is attributed to Louis XIV, although he probably never said it?
14753.e: The sentence “L'État, c'est moi” sums up the idea of absolutism well. But historians think it unlikely that Louis XIV really said it.
14753.m: The sentence “I am the State” fits absolutism but is probably not genuine.

14754.q: Which magnificent palace near Paris did Louis XIV have extended and make his home?
14754.e: Louis XIV had the hunting lodge at Versailles turned into a huge palace with a large park. From 1682 the whole court lived there.
14754.m: Louis XIV made Versailles his magnificent palace.

14755.q: Who ran the government while Louis XIV was still a child?
a: His mother together with a cardinal
A parliament elected by the people
14755.e: Because Louis XIV was still a child, his mother Anne of Austria and Cardinal Mazarin ran the government. After Mazarin’s death in 1661, Louis ruled himself.
14755.m: For the young Louis XIV, his mother and a cardinal ruled.

14756.q: How did Louis XIV control the powerful nobles who had rebelled against the crown in his childhood?
a: He brought them to his court at Versailles
He gave them their own kingdoms
He sent them all to America
14756.e: In Louis’s childhood, nobles had risen against the crown in the Fronde. Later he brought the nobility to his court at Versailles, where he could keep a close eye on them.
14756.m: Louis XIV kept the nobility under control at his court.

14757.q: What did the Reformed Huguenots in France lose under Louis XIV in 1685?
14757.e: The Edict of Nantes of 1598 had allowed the Huguenots to practise their faith. Louis XIV cancelled it in 1685 because only the Catholic faith was to count in France.
14757.m: In 1685 the Huguenots lost their freedom of religion.

14758.q: Where, among other places, did many Huguenots flee from France after 1685?
14758.e: Many Reformed Huguenots fled to Protestant areas, such as Geneva, Bern, Zurich, Basel, the Netherlands and Brandenburg-Prussia. Some brought skills with them, for example for making cloth.
14758.m: Many Huguenots found refuge in Reformed Switzerland.

14759.q: In which art did the young Louis XIV perform himself, among other things dressed as the sun?
14759.e: Louis XIV loved to dance and performed in court ballets. In 1653 he appeared in the “Ballet royal de la nuit” as the rising sun.
14759.m: The young Louis XIV danced in ballets himself.

14760.q: Who followed Louis XIV on the throne after his death in 1715?
14760.e: Louis XIV lived so long that his son and grandson died before him. So his five-year-old great-grandson became king as Louis XV.
14760.m: After Louis XIV, his great-grandson Louis XV became king.

14761.q: From which country did many mercenaries come who served in Louis XIV’s army?
14761.e: France and the Confederation had alliances that allowed mercenaries to be recruited. Swiss regiments and the Hundred Swiss served the French king.
14761.m: Many Swiss served as mercenaries in the French king’s army.

14762.q: Near which city is the Palace of Versailles?
14762.e: Versailles is about 17 kilometres west-south-west of the centre of Paris. Louis XIV made the palace the seat of his court.
14762.m: The Palace of Versailles is near Paris.

14763.q: What stood at Versailles before Louis XIV had the great palace built?
a: A hunting lodge of his father’s
14763.e: Louis XIII had a small hunting lodge at Versailles. Louis XIV had it extended step by step into a huge palace.
14763.m: A hunting lodge became the magnificent Palace of Versailles.

14764.q: What is the most famous room in the Palace of Versailles called?
14764.e: The Hall of Mirrors is a long gallery with many mirrors opposite the windows. It was meant to show the wealth and power of the king.
14764.m: The Hall of Mirrors is the best-known room at Versailles.

14765.q: About how many mirrors does the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles have?
14765.e: The Hall of Mirrors has 357 mirrors spread over 17 arches opposite the windows. Mirrors were very expensive at that time.
14765.m: Over 350 mirrors hang in the Hall of Mirrors.

14766.q: What did Louis XIV make the Palace of Versailles?
a: The seat of his court and government
14766.e: Louis XIV moved to Versailles with his court. From there he ruled all of France.
14766.m: Versailles was the seat of the French court.

14767.q: Why did Louis XIV bring many nobles to his court at Versailles?
14767.e: At court the nobles were watched by the king and kept busy with festivities and ceremonies. So they could not build up power of their own in their provinces.
14767.m: At Versailles Louis XIV kept the nobility under control.

14768.q: Who designed the great gardens of Versailles?
14768.e: The garden designer André Le Nôtre planned the gardens with straight paths, pools and clipped hedges. They are seen as the model of the French Baroque garden.
14768.m: André Le Nôtre created the famous gardens of Versailles.

14769.q: What is typical of a French Baroque garden like the one at Versailles?
14769.e: In a French garden, paths, beds and hedges are laid out symmetrically. Even nature was meant to obey the king’s order.
14769.m: Baroque gardens are laid out strictly geometrically and symmetrically.

14770.q: What were chosen nobles allowed to watch the king doing at Versailles every morning?
14770.e: The king getting up was a solemn ceremony. It was a great honour to be allowed to hand him his shirt, for example.
14770.m: At Versailles even the king getting up was a ceremony.

14771.q: Which empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles in 1871?
14771.e: During the Franco-Prussian War, on 18 January 1871, the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors. For France this was a humiliation.
14771.m: The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871.

14772.q: Which treaty after the First World War was signed in the Hall of Mirrors in 1919?
14772.e: On 28 June 1919 Germany signed the peace treaty in the Hall of Mirrors. France deliberately chose the place where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871.
14772.m: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in the Hall of Mirrors in 1919.

14773.q: What does Herrenchiemsee Palace in Bavaria have to do with Versailles?
a: It was built on the model of Versailles
It was built from stones from Versailles
14773.e: King Ludwig II of Bavaria admired Louis XIV. His palace at Herrenchiemsee even has its own Hall of Mirrors.
14773.m: Herrenchiemsee Palace is a copy of Versailles.

14774.q: Which list is the Palace of Versailles on because it is especially valuable?
a: List of the Wonders of the Ancient World
14774.e: The palace and park of Versailles have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. Millions of people visit the palace every year.
14774.m: Versailles is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

a: The ruler governs alone and without checks.
14775.e: In absolutism the prince has all the power of the state. He is not bound by any laws and does not have to ask anyone’s permission.
14775.m: In absolutism one ruler has all the power.

14776.q: What does it mean that an absolute ruler stood “above the law”?
a: He did not have to obey the laws himself
He was not allowed to make laws
He had every law approved by the people
14776.e: “Absolutism” comes from the Latin “legibus absolutus”, freed from the laws. The ruler made the laws but was not bound by them himself.
14776.m: An absolute ruler stands above the law.

14777.q: How did absolute kings justify their power?
a: With the divine right of kings
14777.e: According to the divine right of kings, God had given the king his power. So the king only had to answer to God, not to the people.
14777.m: Absolute rulers said their power came straight from God.

a: An army that exists even in peacetime
An army that only fights standing up
An army made up only of cavalry
14778.e: In earlier times mercenaries were often hired just for one war. Absolute rulers kept permanently paid soldiers to secure their power.
14778.m: A standing army exists in peacetime too.

14779.q: What was the aim of mercantilism?
a: To export more goods than you import
14779.e: Mercantilism was the economic policy of absolutism. By exporting a lot and importing little, money was to flow into the country and fill the state treasury.
14779.m: Mercantilism aimed to export a lot and import little.

a: A large workshop with division of labour, but mostly handwork
14780.e: In manufactories many people worked in one building, each doing one step of the work. There were hardly any machines yet; much was done by hand.
14780.m: In manufactories many workers shared out the handwork.

14781.q: Which three estates existed in France in the age of absolutism?
a: Clergy, nobility and the Third Estate
14781.e: The First Estate was the clergy, the Second the nobility. The Third Estate was everyone else, meaning peasants, craftsmen and townspeople, and they paid most of the taxes.
14781.m: Society was divided into clergy, nobility and the Third Estate.

14782.q: Why did the French king call a meeting of the three estates in 1789?
a: Because the state had run out of money
Because he wanted a successor elected
Because he wanted to conquer America
14782.e: France was deeply in debt, and the king needed new taxes. The meeting of the Estates-General then led to the French Revolution.
14782.m: The king’s lack of money led to the Revolution in 1789.

14783.q: Which king called himself the “first servant of the state”?
14783.e: Frederick II (the Great) ruled Prussia alone from 1740 to 1786. But he saw himself not as the owner but as the servant of the state.
14783.m: Frederick the Great called himself the first servant of the state.

a: A sole ruler carries out reforms based on ideas of the Enlightenment.
The people elect a king for a fixed time.
The Church takes over the government.
The king hands all power to parliament.
14784.e: Rulers like Frederick II of Prussia or Joseph II of Austria kept sole power. But they carried out reforms, for example in schools, justice and religious tolerance.
14784.m: In enlightened absolutism a sole ruler reforms his state.

14785.q: Which French king is seen as the model of absolutism and is said to have said “I am the State”?
14785.e: Louis XIV reigned from 1643 to 1715 and had the magnificent Palace of Versailles built. He was also called the Sun King.
14785.m: Louis XIV, the Sun King, is the model of absolutism.

14786.q: Who gained more power over the king in England in 1689?
14786.e: With the Bill of Rights, the royal couple had to recognise the rights of Parliament. For example, the king could not raise taxes without Parliament.
14786.m: In England in 1689 Parliament won out against absolutism.

14787.q: Who ruled in Swiss Confederate cities like Bern in the 17th and 18th centuries, where there was no king?
a: A president elected by the people
14787.e: In cities like Bern, Lucerne or Fribourg only a few families had access to government. They were called “Gracious Lords”, and they too ruled rather high-handedly.
14787.m: In cities like Bern a few patrician families ruled.

14788.q: Which country did Galileo Galilei come from?
14788.e: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa in 1564. He worked in Padua and Florence, among other places.
14788.m: Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist.

14789.q: Which instrument did Galileo improve in 1609 and was one of the first to point at the sky?
14789.e: Galileo heard about the newly invented telescope from the Netherlands and built his own, stronger instruments. With them he made important discoveries in the sky.
14789.m: Galileo watched the sky with a telescope he built himself.

14790.q: What did Galileo discover at the planet Jupiter in 1610?
14790.e: Galileo saw four moons circling Jupiter. Today they are called the Galilean moons, and they showed that not everything goes round the Earth.
14790.m: Galileo discovered Jupiter’s four large moons.

14791.q: Which view of the universe did Galileo support?
a: The Earth goes round the Sun.
The Sun goes round the Earth.
The Earth is a flat disc.
The stars go round the Moon.
14791.e: Galileo supported the heliocentric view of Nicolaus Copernicus. At that time the Church still taught that the Earth was at the centre.
14791.m: Galileo taught that the Earth goes round the Sun.

14792.q: What did Galileo have to do in front of the court of the Inquisition in 1633?
14792.e: The Inquisition condemned Galileo for spreading the heliocentric view. He had to renounce it publicly to escape a harsher punishment.
14792.m: In 1633 Galileo had to take back his teaching.

14793.q: What punishment did Galileo receive after his trial, for the rest of his life?
14793.e: After the verdict Galileo lived under house arrest in his country house near Florence. He died there in 1642.
14793.m: Galileo spent his last years under house arrest.

14794.q: Which sentence is Galileo said to have spoken after taking back his teaching, though it is probably a legend?
14794.e: The sentence “Eppur si muove” refers to the Earth. It is not found in any source from Galileo’s lifetime and first appeared in print in 1757, so it is seen as a legend.
14794.m: The sentence “And yet it moves” is probably a legend.

14795.q: What did Galileo see on the Moon with his telescope?
14795.e: At that time people believed heavenly bodies were perfectly smooth. But Galileo saw the shadows of mountains and craters on the Moon.
14795.m: Galileo showed that the Moon has mountains and craters.

14796.q: Which changing shapes of Venus did Galileo observe that disproved the old view of the universe?
14796.e: Galileo saw that Venus waxes and wanes like the Moon. This was best explained if Venus goes round the Sun.
14796.m: The phases of Venus supported the view with the Sun at the centre.

14797.q: What did Galileo find out about free fall, if you leave out air resistance?
a: Bodies always fall at a steady slow speed.
14797.e: Galileo studied falling motion with balls on sloping planes. Without air resistance, heavy and light bodies fall equally fast, which Aristotle had seen differently.
14797.m: Without air resistance all bodies fall equally fast.

14798.q: When did the Catholic Church officially clear Galileo’s name?
14798.e: In 1992 Pope John Paul II declared that condemning Galileo had been a mistake. That was over 350 years after the trial.
14798.m: The Church only admitted in 1992 that condemning Galileo was wrong.

14799.q: Who did Galileo Galilei come into conflict with because of his teaching?
14799.e: Galileo spread the teaching that the Earth goes round the Sun. The Church thought this was wrong and put him on trial.
14799.m: Galileo came into conflict with the Church because of his view of the universe.

14800.q: Which country did Isaac Newton come from?
14800.e: Isaac Newton was born in Woolsthorpe in England. He taught at the University of Cambridge.
14800.m: Isaac Newton was an English scientist.

14801.q: Which force, which keeps the planets in their orbits, did Newton describe with his famous law?
14801.e: Newton realised that the same pulling force makes an apple fall and keeps the Moon going round the Earth. He called it gravitation.
14801.m: Gravity keeps the planets in their orbits.

14802.q: Which well-known story is told about Newton’s idea of gravity?
a: He saw an apple fall from a tree.
He dropped a cannonball from a tower.
14802.e: In old age Newton himself said that a falling apple had set him thinking. The idea that the apple fell on his head is a later embellishment.
14802.m: A falling apple is said to have set Newton thinking about gravity.

14803.q: What did Newton describe in his famous main work of 1687?
a: The laws of motion and gravity
14803.e: The work is known as the “Principia”. In it Newton set out the laws of motion and the law of gravitation.
14803.m: In 1687 Newton described the laws of motion and gravity.

14804.q: What does Newton’s first law, the law of inertia, say?
a: A body stays at rest or in motion if no force acts on it.
14804.e: Without an outside force, a body does not change its motion. That is why a rolling ball only stops at some point because of friction.
14804.m: Without a force, a body does not change its motion.

14805.q: What does Newton’s third law say?
a: For every force there is an equal opposite force.
The Earth is a flat disc.
14805.e: When you push against a wall, the wall pushes back just as hard. The law is also known as “action and reaction”.
14805.m: Every force has an equal opposite force.

14806.q: What did Newton show with a glass prism?
a: White light is made up of many colours.
14806.e: Newton let sunlight pass through a prism and got a band of colours like a rainbow. In this way he showed that white light is made up of the colours of the spectrum.
14806.m: A prism splits white light into its colours.

14807.q: Which kind of telescope was Newton the first to build in a usable form?
14807.e: Instead of lenses, Newton used a curved mirror. That way he avoided the annoying coloured edges that lens telescopes produced.
14807.m: Newton built a telescope with a mirror instead of lenses.

14808.q: In which subject, besides physics, was Newton also a great inventor?
14808.e: Newton developed new methods of calculation that were needed for physics. At the same time as the German Leibniz, he invented a new kind of mathematics.
14808.m: Newton was also a great mathematician.

14809.q: What does the physical unit “newton” stand for?
14809.e: In honour of Isaac Newton, force is measured in newtons. One newton is about the weight of a 100-gram bar of chocolate.
14809.m: Force is measured in the unit newton.

14810.q: Roughly when did Isaac Newton live?
14810.e: Newton lived from 1643 to 1727. He is one of the great researchers at the beginning of modern science.

14811.q: Why is Newton considered one of the greatest scientists?
a: He explained motion on Earth and in the sky with the same laws
He built the first steam locomotive
14811.e: Newton showed that the same gravity makes an apple fall and keeps the planets in their orbits. This changed people’s view of the world.
14811.m: Newton’s laws apply on Earth and in space.

14812.q: Where was Isaac Newton buried in 1727?
a: In St Peter’s Basilica in Rome
14812.e: Newton was buried with great honour in Westminster Abbey in London. Many famous people of Great Britain lie there.
14812.m: Newton is buried in Westminster Abbey.

14813.q: In which century did the Enlightenment reach its peak in Europe?
14813.e: The Enlightenment began in the late 17th century and shaped above all the 18th century. This time is also called the “Age of Reason”.
14813.m: The Enlightenment shaped above all the 18th century.

14814.q: According to the ideas of the Enlightenment, what should people mainly rely on?
14814.e: The thinkers of the Enlightenment wanted to overcome superstition and blind obedience. Everything was to be tested with one’s own mind.
14814.m: The Enlightenment put its trust in human reason.

14815.q: Which German philosopher explained in 1784 that enlightenment is “man’s emergence from his self-incurred immaturity”?
14815.e: Immanuel Kant wrote this in his essay “An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?”. Someone is immature if they do not think for themselves but let others guide them.
14815.m: For Kant, enlightenment meant thinking for yourself.

14816.q: What does the Enlightenment motto “Sapere aude” mean?
a: Have the courage to use your own understanding.
14816.e: Kant made the Latin saying the motto of the Enlightenment. Word for word it means something like “Dare to be wise”.
14816.m: “Sapere aude” calls on you to think for yourself with courage.

14817.q: What is the great reference work of the French Enlightenment, published by Diderot and d'Alembert, called?
14817.e: The Encyclopédie appeared in many volumes from 1751. It aimed to collect the knowledge of the time and make it available to many people.
14817.m: The Encyclopédie collected the knowledge of the Enlightenment.

14818.q: Which French thinker called for the separation of powers in “The Spirit of the Laws” in 1748?
14818.e: Montesquieu wanted to share power in the state between different bodies. This was to stop any one person from becoming too powerful.
14818.m: Montesquieu is seen as the father of the separation of powers.

14819.q: Which three powers are distinguished in the separation of powers?
14819.e: The legislative power makes laws, the executive carries them out and the judiciary judges. In Switzerland these are the Federal Assembly, the Federal Council and the Federal Supreme Court.
14819.m: The separation of powers divides lawmaking, government and the courts.

14820.q: In and near which present-day Swiss city did the Enlightenment thinker Voltaire live for many years?
14820.e: From 1755 Voltaire lived on the estate “Les Délices” in Geneva and later, until his death, in Ferney, just across the French border near Geneva. From there he wrote against intolerance and injustice.
14820.m: Voltaire lived in and near Geneva for a long time.

14821.q: Which natural rights of every human being did the English philosopher John Locke name?
14821.e: John Locke believed every person has these rights by nature. The state exists to protect them.
14821.m: According to John Locke, everyone has a right to life, liberty and property.

14823.q: Albrecht von Haller from Bern wrote the poem “The Alps”. What did he praise in it?
a: The simple life of mountain farmers
14823.e: Albrecht von Haller was a doctor, scientist and poet. In “The Alps” he praised the simple life of the mountain people and made the Alps known all over Europe.
14823.m: In “The Alps” Haller praised the simple life in the mountains.

14824.q: Which Swiss educator, inspired by the Enlightenment, worked for the education of poor children?
14824.e: Pestalozzi looked after orphans, for example in Stans, and later ran an institute in Yverdon. He wanted to educate head, heart and hand equally.
14824.m: Pestalozzi wanted all children to get a good education.

14825.q: Which woman was executed in Glarus in 1782 and is often called the last “witch” in Europe?
14825.e: Anna Göldi was condemned in an unfair trial, which Enlightenment thinkers criticised even then. She is considered the last woman in Europe executed for witchcraft after a court verdict; in 2008 the canton of Glarus cleared her name.
14825.m: Anna Göldi was the victim of an unjust trial in 1782.

14826.q: In which city was Jean-Jacques Rousseau born in 1712?
14826.e: Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712. He liked to call himself a “citizen of Geneva”.

14827.q: What did Rousseau think about in his book “The Social Contract”?
a: What a fair state should look like
14827.e: In “The Social Contract” of 1762, Rousseau asks what a state should look like in which people stay free. The book influenced the French Revolution.
14827.m: Rousseau thought about a fair state.

14828.q: According to Rousseau, from whom should power in the state come?
14828.e: Rousseau stood for the sovereignty of the people. Laws should match the general will (“volonté générale”) of all citizens.
14828.m: According to Rousseau, all power comes from the people.

14830.q: What is Rousseau’s book “Emile” of 1762 about?
14830.e: “Emile, or On Education” tells how a boy is brought up close to nature. The book later influenced educators such as Pestalozzi.
14830.m: In “Emile” Rousseau describes his ideas on education.

14831.q: Which slogan is often linked with Rousseau, although it does not appear in his works in that form?
14831.e: Rousseau praised the natural, simple life and criticised civilisation. The short slogan “Back to nature” sums this up, but the exact words are not his.
14831.m: The slogan “Back to nature” sums up Rousseau’s thinking, but the exact words are not his.

14832.q: What happened to Rousseau’s books “Emile” and “The Social Contract” in Paris and Geneva in 1762?
14832.e: The authorities saw the books as an attack on Church and state. In Geneva both books were burned, in Paris “Emile”, and Rousseau had to flee to avoid arrest.
14832.m: Rousseau’s books were banned in 1762 and he had to flee.

14833.q: On which island in Lake Biel did Rousseau find refuge for a few weeks in 1765?
14833.e: After fleeing, Rousseau first lived in Môtiers in the Neuchâtel Jura and then on St Peter’s Island. He later described his time there as one of the happiest of his life.
14833.m: In 1765 Rousseau lived on St Peter’s Island in Lake Biel.

14834.q: On which lake is Rousseau’s famous love story set?
14834.e: The novel in letters “Julie, or the New Heloise” was published in 1761 and is set on Lake Geneva. It was one of the most widely read novels of its time.
14834.m: Rousseau’s love story is set on Lake Geneva.

14835.q: In his writing on inequality, what did Rousseau see as one origin of inequality among people?
14835.e: Rousseau believed inequality began when someone fenced off a piece of land and said “This is mine”. This led to quarrels and dependence.
14835.m: For Rousseau, property was one origin of inequality.

14836.q: Which honour did Rousseau receive after the French Revolution?
a: He was buried in the Panthéon in Paris.
He became President of the USA.
14836.e: The revolutionaries saw Rousseau as an important thinker who paved the way. In 1794 his remains were moved to the Panthéon, where great figures of France lie.
14836.m: Rousseau was buried in the Panthéon in 1794.

14837.q: Was Geneva part of the Swiss Confederation in Rousseau’s lifetime?
a: No, Geneva was a republic of its own.
Yes, Geneva had been a canton since 1291.
14837.e: Geneva was an independent city republic and allied with Confederate cantons. Geneva only became a Swiss canton in 1815.
14837.m: Geneva only became a Swiss canton in 1815.

14838.q: When did the French National Assembly proclaim the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen?
14838.e: The Declaration was passed on 26 August 1789, shortly after the start of the French Revolution. It states that people are born free and equal in rights.
14838.m: France declared the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in 1789.

14839.q: Which organisation works worldwide for prisoners and human rights and has a candle in barbed wire as its symbol?
14839.e: Amnesty International was founded in 1961. It draws attention to human rights abuses and helps people imprisoned for their opinions.
14839.m: Amnesty International fights for human rights worldwide.

14840.q: Which statement is in the American Declaration of Independence of 1776?
a: The king is appointed by God.
14840.e: The Declaration of Independence of 4 July 1776, written mainly by Thomas Jefferson, names rights such as life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. But at that time these rights did not apply to enslaved people.
14840.m: The American Declaration of Independence says all men are created equal.

14841.q: Which Frenchwoman wrote a “Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen” in 1791?
14841.e: Olympe de Gouges criticised the 1789 Declaration for not treating women equally. She demanded the same rights for women and men.
14841.m: As early as 1791 Olympe de Gouges demanded equal rights for women.

14842.q: When did the UN adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
14842.e: After the crimes of the Second World War, the UN General Assembly in Paris passed this declaration. That is why 10 December is now Human Rights Day.
14842.m: The UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

14843.q: How many articles does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 have?
14843.e: The Declaration has 30 articles. The first says, in essence, that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
14843.m: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights has 30 articles.

14844.q: Who led the UN commission that drew up the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
14844.e: Eleanor Roosevelt, the widow of US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, chaired the Human Rights Commission. She worked hard for the Declaration.
14844.m: Eleanor Roosevelt led the work on the Declaration of Human Rights.

14845.q: In which city is the European Court of Human Rights based?
14845.e: The court in Strasbourg watches over the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). People from Switzerland can also complain there.
14845.m: The European Court of Human Rights is in Strasbourg.

14846.q: What is the treaty called by which Switzerland and other European countries have committed themselves to protecting human rights?
14846.e: Switzerland joined the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) in 1974. Since then people in Switzerland can turn to the court in Strasbourg.
14846.m: With the ECHR Switzerland has committed itself to protecting human rights.

14847.q: In which Swiss city does the UN Human Rights Council meet?
14847.e: The United Nations Human Rights Council was founded in 2006 and is based in Geneva. Geneva is an important place for international organisations.
14847.m: The UN Human Rights Council is based in Geneva.

14848.q: What does Article 4 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights forbid?
14848.e: Article 4 states that no one may be held in slavery or servitude. Slavery and the slave trade are banned in all their forms.
14848.m: Under human rights, no one may be enslaved.

14849.q: What was the name of the French king at the start of the Revolution?
14849.e: Louis XVI had been King of France since 1774. He was deposed in 1792 and executed in 1793.
14849.m: Louis XVI was the king the Revolution turned against.

14850.q: Which group formed the First Estate in France before 1789?
14850.e: Society was divided into three estates. The First Estate was the clergy, the Second the nobility and the Third everyone else.
14850.m: The clergy formed the First Estate.

14851.q: Who belonged to the Third Estate before the Revolution?
14851.e: The Third Estate included peasants, craftsmen, merchants and other townspeople. It made up well over 90 per cent of the population but had little power.
14851.m: The Third Estate was the great majority of the people.

14852.q: Which problem led the king to call the Estates-General, which met in 1789?
a: A plague was raging in the country.
A war against England had been lost.
14852.e: France had huge debts, partly because of wars and the expensive court. The king needed new taxes, so in August 1788 he called the Estates-General, which met in May 1789.
14852.m: The high state debts helped trigger the Revolution.

14853.q: What did the deputies of the Third Estate swear in the Tennis Court Oath on 20 June 1789?
a: Not to separate until France had a constitution
To obey the king for ever
14853.e: The deputies had declared themselves the National Assembly. In the tennis court hall at Versailles they swore to stay together until a constitution had been written.
14853.m: In the Tennis Court Oath the deputies promised to create a constitution.

14854.q: What is the famous motto of the French Revolution?
a: All for one, one for all
14854.e: In French the motto is “Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité”. It is still the motto of the French Republic today.
14854.m: Liberty, equality and fraternity are the motto of the Revolution.

14855.q: What was abolished on the night of 4 to 5 August 1789?
a: Many privileges of the nobility and clergy
14855.e: In this night session the nobility and clergy gave up many old privileges. Serfdom ended at once, but the peasants first had to buy themselves out of many other dues until these were fully abolished in 1793.
14855.m: In August 1789 the nobility and clergy gave up many old privileges.

14856.q: Where was the royal family taken after the women’s march in October 1789?
14856.e: On 5 October 1789, mostly women marched from Paris to Versailles. They forced the king to move to Paris with his family.
14856.m: After the women’s march the king had to live in Paris.

14857.q: What did Louis XVI try to do in June 1791 in the flight to Varennes?
14857.e: On the night of 21 June 1791 the king fled Paris in disguise with his family, heading for a fortress near the border. In Varennes he was recognised and brought back, and after that many French people no longer trusted him.
14857.m: The failed flight to Varennes cost the king much trust.

14858.q: In which year did France become a republic?
14858.e: In September 1792 the National Convention met and abolished the monarchy. With that, France became a republic for the first time.

14859.q: When was King Louis XVI executed?
14859.e: The National Convention condemned the deposed king for treason. On 21 January 1793 he was executed by guillotine in Paris.

14860.q: With which device were many people executed during the Revolution?
14860.e: The guillotine is a falling blade. It is named after the doctor Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, who had called for a quick method of execution.
14860.m: The guillotine became the symbol of the revolutionary period.

14861.q: What is the period from 1793 to 1794 called, in which many supposed enemies of the Revolution were executed?
14861.e: Under the Committee of Public Safety, thousands of people were condemned as enemies of the Revolution. This time is called the Reign of Terror or “Terreur”.
14861.m: The Reign of Terror was the cruellest phase of the Revolution.

14862.q: Which Jacobin led the Reign of Terror and was executed himself in 1794?
14862.e: Robespierre was the leading figure of the Committee of Public Safety. In July 1794 he was overthrown and executed by guillotine the next day.
