14862.m: Robespierre stood for the Reign of Terror and in the end fell victim to it himself.

14863.q: What in Lucerne commemorates the Swiss Guards who fell in the storming of the Tuileries in Paris in 1792?
14863.e: On 10 August 1792 Swiss Guards defended the royal palace, and many died. The Lion Monument in Lucerne was unveiled in 1821 in their memory.
14863.m: The Lion Monument in Lucerne honours the fallen Swiss Guards.

14864.q: On which day was the Bastille stormed?
14864.e: On 14 July 1789 a crowd in Paris stormed the Bastille fortress. This event is seen as the symbol of the start of the Revolution.
14864.m: The Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789.

14865.q: In which city did the Bastille stand?
14865.e: The Bastille was an old fortress in the east of Paris. Today the square where it stood recalls it.

14866.q: What was the Bastille mainly used for before the Revolution?
14866.e: The Bastille served the king as a prison. People could be locked up there without a court verdict, so it was seen as a sign of tyranny.
14866.m: The Bastille was a prison and a symbol of oppression.

14867.q: What were the rebels mainly looking for in the Bastille?
14867.e: The crowd had already taken guns from the Hôtel des Invalides. In the Bastille they wanted to get at the stores of powder and ammunition.
14867.m: The rebels wanted to get powder for their guns from the Bastille.

14868.q: How many prisoners were still in the Bastille when it was stormed?
14868.e: Only seven prisoners were freed, among them forgers and mentally ill people. So the storming mattered above all as a symbol.
14868.m: In 1789 there were only seven prisoners left in the Bastille.

14869.q: What is 14 July in France today?
14869.e: Since 1880, 14 July has been the French national holiday. It recalls the storming of the Bastille and the unity of the nation.

14870.q: Which dismissal by the king angered the people of Paris shortly before the storming of the Bastille?
a: The dismissal of the finance minister Necker
The dismissal of the Swiss Guard
14870.e: Jacques Necker was popular with the people. When the king dismissed him on 11 July 1789, many Parisians feared a blow against the National Assembly.
14870.m: Necker’s dismissal stirred up feeling in Paris.

14871.q: What happened to the Bastille building after it was stormed?
a: It was turned into a church.
14871.e: As early as 16 July 1789 people began to pull down the fortress. Stones from the Bastille were even sold as souvenirs.
14871.m: The Bastille was torn down after it was stormed.

14872.q: What happened to the commander of the Bastille after it was stormed?
a: He was killed by the crowd
14872.e: Bernard-René de Launay was the commander of the Bastille. After he surrendered, he was killed by the crowd on the way to the town hall.
14872.m: The commander of the Bastille did not survive the storming.

14873.q: Why is the storming of the Bastille seen as so important?
a: It became a symbol of the people’s victory over the king’s tyranny.
14873.e: In military terms the capture was small, but it showed that the people could stand up to royal power. That is why it became the symbol of the Revolution.
14873.m: The storming of the Bastille is above all a symbol of the Revolution.

14874.q: What did the crowd fetch on the morning of 14 July 1789 before marching to the Bastille?
14874.e: Many guns were stored in a home for war veterans, the Hôtel des Invalides. The crowd took them and then marched to the Bastille to get powder.
14874.m: The crowd first fetched guns, then wanted powder.

14875.q: Roughly how many attackers died in the storming of the Bastille?
14875.e: A little over 90 people died on the side of the attackers, and only a few on the side of the defenders. The fighting lasted only a few hours.
14875.m: About 100 attackers died in the storming of the Bastille.

14876.q: In which year was the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen passed in France?
14876.e: The National Assembly passed the Declaration in August 1789, a few weeks after the storming of the Bastille. It is seen as the first declaration of human rights in Europe.
14876.m: The Rights of Man and of the Citizen were declared in 1789.

14877.q: What does Article 1 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen say?
a: People are born free and equal in rights.
14877.e: Article 1 begins with the sentence: “Men are born and remain free and equal in rights.” With this the Declaration turned against the privileges of the estates.
14877.m: All people are born free and equal in rights.

14878.q: In which country was the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen written in 1789?
14878.e: The Declaration was written in 1789 at the beginning of the French Revolution. It states that all people are born free and equal in rights.
14878.m: The Declaration of Rights of 1789 comes from France.

14879.q: Which thinkers especially influenced the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen?
a: The knights of the Middle Ages
14879.e: Enlightenment thinkers such as Montesquieu and Rousseau had written about liberty, equality and the separation of powers. Their ideas went into the Declaration.
14879.m: The ideas of the Enlightenment shaped the Declaration of Rights.

14881.q: Which group was shut out of many rights in the 1789 Declaration, especially the right to vote?
14881.e: The Declaration spoke of “men”, and when it came to political rights it really did mean mostly men. Women, for example, were not allowed to vote.
14881.m: In 1789 women did not get the same political rights as men.

14882.q: Which woman wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen in 1791?
14882.e: Olympe de Gouges demanded full equality between women and men. She was executed in 1793 during the Reign of Terror.
14882.m: Olympe de Gouges fought early on for women’s rights.

14883.q: What does the presumption of innocence, which is in the 1789 Declaration, mean?
a: Everyone counts as innocent until convicted.
Anyone who stays silent is guilty.
14883.e: Article 9 of the Declaration states that a person counts as innocent until they are convicted. This principle still applies in Switzerland today.
14883.m: No one counts as guilty before a court has convicted them.

14884.q: Which freedom does the 1789 Declaration protect, among others?
a: Freedom to carry weapons without rules
14884.e: Articles 10 and 11 allow people to say, write and print their opinions freely. Anyone who misuses this freedom must answer for it before the law.
14884.m: The Declaration of Rights protects free speech.

14885.q: According to Article 16 of the Declaration, what does a state need in order to have a real constitution?
a: Guaranteed rights and the separation of powers
14885.e: Article 16 says that a society without guaranteed rights and without separation of powers has no constitution. The idea of the separation of powers comes from Montesquieu.
14885.m: The separation of powers is part of every real constitution.

14886.q: Which right does the 1789 Declaration call “inviolable and sacred”?
14886.e: Article 17 protects property. The state may only take it away when there is a public need and with fair compensation.
14886.m: Property is specially protected in the 1789 Declaration.

14887.q: What does the term “human rights” mean?
a: Rights that every person has from birth
Rights that only citizens of a country have
Rights that only the king grants
14887.e: Human rights apply to all people, whatever their origin, class or wealth. They do not have to be earned first.
14887.m: Every person has human rights from birth.

14888.q: Which country had written down its own rights for its citizens shortly before 1789 and was a model for France?
14888.e: The Americans had declared their independence from England in 1776 and written down basic rights. Many French people knew these texts and were inspired by them.
14888.m: The American basic rights were a model for France.

14889.q: On which island was Napoleon Bonaparte born?
14889.e: Napoleon was born on 15 August 1769 in Ajaccio on Corsica. Corsica had only recently become part of France.

14890.q: Roughly how old was Napoleon when he became emperor in 1804?
14890.e: Napoleon was born on Corsica in 1769. So at his coronation in 1804 he was only 35 years old.

14891.q: Which office did Napoleon take after his coup of 1799?
14891.e: In November 1799 Napoleon overthrew the Directory. The new constitution made him First Consul and so the most powerful man in France.

14892.q: In which year did Napoleon crown himself Emperor of the French?
14892.e: The grand coronation took place on 2 December 1804 in Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris. With that, the republic became an empire.
14892.m: Napoleon became Emperor of the French in 1804.

14893.q: What special thing did Napoleon do at his coronation as emperor?
a: He put the crown on his own head.
He had himself crowned in Rome.
He had himself crowned by the English king.
14893.e: Pope Pius VII was at the coronation. But Napoleon put the crown on himself to show that he owed his power to no one.

14894.q: What is the code of law that Napoleon introduced in 1804 called?
14894.e: The Code civil regulated civil law, for example property, family and contracts. It became a model in many countries in Europe.
14894.m: The Code civil was Napoleon’s most important code of law.

14895.q: Which kind of equality did the Code civil guarantee?
a: Equality of all citizens before the law
Equal wealth for rich and poor
Equality of all religions with the state
14895.e: With the Code civil there were no more special rights for nobles. All male citizens were equal before the law, although women remained at a disadvantage.
14895.m: The Code civil made citizens equal before the law.

14896.q: What was the name of Napoleon’s first wife?
14896.e: Napoleon married Joséphine in 1796. Because the marriage remained childless, he divorced her in 1809.

14897.q: Why did Napoleon marry Marie-Louise, the daughter of the Austrian emperor, in 1810?
a: He wanted an heir and a link to an old ruling house.
He wanted to declare war on Austria.
She was his childhood sweetheart from Corsica.
The Pope had ordered him to.
14897.e: Napoleon needed a son as his successor. The marriage to Marie-Louise also linked him to the House of Habsburg; in 1811 their son Napoleon II was born.
14897.m: With the marriage of 1810 Napoleon was seeking an heir and prestige.

14898.q: To which country did Napoleon lead a campaign in 1798 on which scientists also travelled?
14898.e: With the Egyptian campaign Napoleon wanted to disrupt Great Britain’s route to India. Scholars who came along studied the country, and the Rosetta Stone was found.
14898.m: In 1798 Napoleon led a campaign to Egypt.

14899.q: To which island was Napoleon first exiled in 1814?
14899.e: After giving up the throne in April 1814, Napoleon had to go to the Mediterranean island of Elba. In spring 1815 he secretly returned to France.
14899.m: Napoleon’s first exile took him to Elba.

14900.q: What is Napoleon’s short return to power in 1815 called?
14900.e: Napoleon landed in France on 1 March 1815 and took power again. After his defeat at Waterloo he finally gave up the throne in June.
14900.m: The Hundred Days were Napoleon’s last attempt to stay in power.

14901.q: On which island in the Atlantic did Napoleon die in 1821?
14901.e: After the defeat at Waterloo the British exiled Napoleon to the remote island of St Helena in the South Atlantic. He died there in 1821.
14901.m: Napoleon died in exile on St Helena in 1821.

14902.e: In 1840 Napoleon’s remains were brought from St Helena to Paris. Since then he has rested in a sarcophagus in the dome of Les Invalides.
14902.m: Napoleon’s tomb is in Les Invalides in Paris.

14903.q: Which branch of the army did Napoleon train in as a young officer?
14903.e: At a military school Napoleon was trained as an artillery officer, the troops with the cannons. This made him known at the siege of Toulon in 1793. There was no air force yet at that time.
14903.m: Napoleon began his career as an artillery officer.

14904.q: How did Napoleon come to power in 1799?
14904.e: On 18 Brumaire in the revolutionary calendar, 9 November 1799, Napoleon overthrew the government with the help of soldiers. After that he became First Consul.
14904.m: Napoleon came to power through a coup in 1799.

14905.q: In which battle did Napoleon defeat Austria and Russia in 1805?
14905.e: On 2 December 1805, exactly a year after his coronation, Napoleon defeated the armies of Austria and Russia at Austerlitz. It is seen as one of his greatest victories.
14905.m: At Austerlitz in 1805 Napoleon won a great victory.

14906.q: In which sea battle did the British fleet under Nelson defeat the French fleet in 1805?
14906.e: On 21 October 1805 Admiral Nelson destroyed the French and Spanish fleet at Trafalgar. Nelson himself was killed in the battle.
14906.m: At Trafalgar in 1805 Great Britain secured its rule over the seas.

a: A trade ban against Great Britain
14907.e: With the Berlin Decree of 1806 Napoleon banned trade with Great Britain. He wanted to weaken the British economy, because he could not conquer the island by force.
14907.m: The Continental System was meant to harm Great Britain’s economy.

14908.q: Which old empire came to an end in 1806 as a result of Napoleon’s successes?
14908.e: In 1806 many German princes joined together in the Confederation of the Rhine under Napoleon and left the empire. Emperor Francis II then laid down the imperial crown.
14908.m: The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806.

14909.q: In which year did Napoleon march against Russia with the Grande Armée?
14909.e: In June 1812 Napoleon’s huge army crossed the border into Russia. The campaign ended in disaster.
14909.m: The Russian campaign took place in 1812.

14910.q: Which city did Napoleon capture in September 1812, without Russia giving up?
14910.e: Napoleon entered Moscow on 14 September 1812. But the Tsar did not negotiate, and because supplies were lacking, the army had to retreat in October.
14910.m: Capturing Moscow did not bring Napoleon the victory he hoped for.

14911.q: What happened to Napoleon’s army on the retreat from Russia in the winter of 1812?
a: The vast majority of soldiers died or were captured.
It conquered Sweden on the way.
It was taken home by ship.
14911.e: Cold, hunger, disease and attacks destroyed the Grande Armée. Of several hundred thousand soldiers, only a small part returned.
14911.m: The retreat from Russia was a disaster for Napoleon’s army.

14912.q: On which river did Swiss regiments fight in November 1812 to cover the retreat of the Grande Armée?
14912.e: On the Berezina in today’s Belarus, Swiss soldiers protected the army’s crossing. Of about 1,300 Swiss, only about 300 were left at roll call afterwards.
14912.m: On the Berezina the Swiss regiments suffered heavy losses in 1812.

14913.q: What does the Berezina Song in Switzerland remind people of?
a: Swiss soldiers in Napoleon’s Russian campaign
The founding of the Swiss Confederation
The building of the Gotthard tunnel
14913.e: On the Berezina, Swiss regiments covered the retreat of Napoleon’s army in November 1812. An officer is said to have sung the song “Our life is like a journey” before the fight, and it has been called the Berezina Song ever since.
14913.m: The Berezina Song remembers the Swiss at the Berezina.

14914.q: What is the great battle near Leipzig in October 1813 called?
14914.e: From 16 to 19 October 1813, soldiers from many nations fought each other. Russia, Prussia, Austria and Sweden defeated Napoleon.
14914.m: The Battle of the Nations at Leipzig in 1813 was a decisive defeat for Napoleon.

14915.q: In which present-day country is Waterloo, where Napoleon was finally defeated in 1815?
14915.e: Waterloo is about 15 kilometres south of Brussels in today’s Belgium. At that time the area belonged to the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
14915.m: The Battle of Waterloo took place in today’s Belgium.

14916.q: When did the Battle of Waterloo take place?
14916.e: On 18 June 1815 Napoleon lost at Waterloo to the British and Prussians. A few days later he gave up the throne for good.
14916.m: Napoleon was beaten at Waterloo on 18 June 1815.

14917.q: Which commanders defeated Napoleon at Waterloo?
14917.e: The British Duke of Wellington held out against the French army. The Prussian troops under Blücher arrived in time and decided the battle.
14917.m: Wellington and Blücher defeated Napoleon at Waterloo.

14918.q: In which country did the people fight a “little war”, a so-called guerrilla war, against the French from 1808?
14918.e: In 1808 Napoleon made his brother Joseph King of Spain. Many Spaniards fought back with small, mobile fighting groups, and that is where the word guerrilla comes from.
14918.m: Spanish resistance gave the word “guerrilla” its meaning.

14919.q: What are the wars called in which European states repeatedly allied against France from 1792 to 1815?
14919.e: A coalition is an alliance. Several times countries like Austria, Prussia, Russia and Great Britain joined together against France.
14919.m: In the Coalition Wars allied states fought against France.

14920.q: Which country marched into the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1798?
14920.e: At the beginning of 1798 French troops occupied Switzerland. The Old Swiss Confederacy collapsed.
14920.m: French troops ended the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1798.

14921.q: From when to when did the Helvetic Republic exist?
14921.e: The Helvetic Republic was founded in April 1798. It ended in March 1803 with Napoleon’s Act of Mediation.
14921.m: The Helvetic Republic existed from 1798 to 1803.

14922.q: In which town was the Helvetic Republic proclaimed on 12 April 1798?
14922.e: In Aarau, representatives from ten cantons met and founded the Helvetic Republic. Aarau then became its first capital.
14922.m: The Helvetic Republic was founded in Aarau in 1798.

14923.q: How was the Helvetic Republic organised?
a: As a single unified state on the French model
As a loose alliance of independent cantons
As part of the Holy Roman Empire
14923.e: The cantons lost their independence and became mere administrative districts. The government decided centrally for the whole country.
14923.m: The Helvetic Republic was a centrally governed unified state.

14924.q: Which man from Basel wrote the first Helvetic constitution on France’s behalf?
14924.e: Peter Ochs drafted the constitution for the French Directory. Opponents mockingly called it the “Ochsenbüchlein”, the little ox book.
14924.m: Peter Ochs wrote the constitution of the Helvetic Republic.

14925.q: Which area was freed from Bernese rule in 1798?
14925.e: Vaud had long been a subject territory of Bern. With France’s help it became free in 1798 and is now a canton of its own.
14925.m: Vaud became independent of Bern in 1798.

14926.q: What happened to the subject territories in the Helvetic Republic?
a: They had to pay higher dues.
14926.e: Before, individual cantons ruled over subject territories such as Aargau or Ticino. In the Helvetic Republic all citizens had equal rights.
14926.m: The Helvetic Republic turned subjects into citizens with equal rights.

14927.q: What three colours did the flag of the Helvetic Republic have?
14927.e: The Helvetic Republic used a tricolour in green, red and yellow. The white cross on a red background of today was not the national flag at that time.
14927.m: The Helvetic flag was green, red and yellow.

14928.q: In which battle were the Bernese defeated by the French on 5 March 1798?
14928.e: At Grauholz north of Bern the Bernese troops were beaten. The city of Bern fell on the same day.
14928.m: After the Battle of Grauholz, Bern fell to the French in 1798.

14929.q: What did the French take away after conquering Bern in 1798?
a: The clock of the Zytglogge tower
14929.e: Bern was very rich. The French seized the state treasure and took it to France.
14929.m: In 1798 France stole Bern’s rich state treasure.

14930.q: Which area resisted the French and the new constitution especially fiercely in September 1798?
14930.e: Many people in Nidwalden refused to swear the oath to the Helvetic constitution. French troops crushed the resistance bloodily in September 1798.
14930.m: Nidwalden put up fierce resistance to the French in 1798.

14931.q: Which educator looked after orphans in Stans in 1799?
14931.e: After the fighting in Nidwalden there were many orphans. In 1799 Pestalozzi ran an orphanage in Stans and later became world-famous as an educator.
14931.m: In 1799 Pestalozzi cared for orphans in Stans.

14932.q: Which armies fought against France on Swiss soil in 1799?
14932.e: In the Second Coalition War, Switzerland became a battleground. There were two battles at Zurich in 1799, and the Russian general Suvorov crossed the Alps.
14932.m: In 1799 Switzerland became a battlefield for foreign armies.

14933.q: What is the uprising of 1802 called, in which opponents drove out the Helvetic government?
14933.e: The rebels were often armed only with sticks, “Steckli” in Swiss German, so it is known as the War of the Sticks. They drove the government out of Bern, after which Napoleon stepped in.
14933.m: The Stecklikrieg brought down the Helvetic Republic in 1802.

14934.q: What was the name of Napoleon’s act of 1803 that replaced the Helvetic Republic?
14934.e: Napoleon mediated between the quarrelling Swiss; “mediation” means acting as a go-between. The Act of Mediation of 19 February 1803 created a union of cantons once again.
14934.m: The Act of Mediation ended the Helvetic Republic in 1803.

14935.q: When did the Congress of Vienna meet?
14935.e: The Congress began in Vienna in September 1814. The Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815.
14935.m: The Congress of Vienna met in 1814 and 1815.

14936.q: What was the aim of the Congress of Vienna?
a: To reorganise Europe after Napoleon’s defeat
14936.e: After the Napoleonic Wars, borders and rulers in Europe had to be set again. For this, representatives of almost all European states met in Vienna.
14936.m: The Congress of Vienna reorganised Europe after Napoleon.

14937.q: Which Austrian statesman led the Congress of Vienna?
14937.e: Metternich was the Austrian foreign minister. He strongly shaped the Congress and European politics in the decades that followed.
14937.m: Metternich was the host and leader of the Congress of Vienna.

14938.q: What does the term “Restoration”, which stands for the time after the Congress of Vienna, mean?
14938.e: The princes wanted to bring back the conditions before the Revolution as far as possible. Many old ruling houses returned to power.
14938.m: Restoration means bringing back the old order.

14939.q: What was the “balance of power” in Europe meant to prevent?
a: One single state ruling all of Europe
The great powers negotiating with each other
France being ruled by a king again
14939.e: After Napoleon’s dominance, the great powers wanted none of them to become too strong. This was meant to keep the peace.
14939.m: The balance of power was meant to prevent a new domination.

14940.q: Which saying describes the many balls and parties during the Congress of Vienna?
a: “The Congress dances, but it does not move forward.”
14940.e: Besides the negotiations, there were many parties in Vienna. That is why Prince Charles Joseph de Ligne joked that the Congress danced but did not move forward.
14940.m: At the Congress of Vienna there was a lot of partying and slow negotiating.

14941.q: What did the great powers recognise for Switzerland in 1815?
14941.e: The great powers recognised Switzerland’s independence and permanent neutrality. The declaration was signed in Paris on 20 November 1815.
14941.m: Since 1815 Switzerland’s neutrality has been recognised internationally.

14942.q: Which three cantons newly joined the Confederation after the Congress of Vienna?
14942.e: The great powers agreed that Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva would become cantons. This gave Switzerland 22 cantons.
14942.m: Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva became Swiss cantons in 1815.

14943.q: Which area became part of the canton of Bern in 1815?
14943.e: Bern had lost Vaud and Aargau. In return it got most of the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel, that is, the Jura. Part of it became the canton of Jura in 1979.

14944.q: Which area that once belonged to the Grisons did Switzerland finally lose at the Congress of Vienna?
14944.e: Valtellina had long been a subject territory of the Three Leagues. At the Congress of Vienna it was finally given to Austria, and today it belongs to Italy.

14945.q: Why did the great powers agree to a neutral Switzerland in 1815?
a: It separated France and Austria as a buffer
It had the strongest army in Europe
It supplied all the great powers with gold
It was Napoleon’s most important ally
14945.e: A neutral Switzerland lay like a buffer between France and Austria. No great power could use the Alpine passes for itself alone. Diplomats like Charles Pictet de Rochemont from Geneva argued for this.
14945.m: Neutral Switzerland served the great powers as a buffer.

14946.q: Which alliance did Russia, Austria and Prussia form in September 1815?
14946.e: The three monarchs promised to rule according to Christian principles and to protect the old order. Great Britain did not join the alliance.
14946.m: The Holy Alliance was meant to secure the rule of the monarchs.

14947.q: Which treaty held the cantons together from 1815 to 1848?
14947.e: The Federal Treaty was sworn in the Grossmünster in Zurich in 1815. It was a loose union of the cantons and lasted until the Federal Constitution of 1848.
14947.m: The Federal Treaty applied from 1815 to 1848.

14948.q: In which year did the Catholic conservative cantons join together in the Sonderbund?
14948.e: In December 1845 seven Catholic conservative cantons founded a secret defensive alliance, the Sonderbund.

14949.q: Which of these cantons belonged to the Sonderbund?
14949.e: Lucerne was even the leading canton of the Sonderbund. Zurich, Bern and Aargau were on the liberal side.
14949.m: Lucerne was the most important canton in the Sonderbund.

14950.q: How many cantons made up the Sonderbund?
14950.e: Seven Catholic conservative cantons joined together. Obwalden and Nidwalden counted together as one canton (Unterwalden).
14950.m: Seven Catholic cantons formed the Sonderbund.

14951.q: Which of these cantons was NOT a member of the Sonderbund?
14951.e: Ticino was Catholic but did not join the Sonderbund. Valais, Fribourg and Zug were members.
14951.m: Catholic Ticino stayed out of the Sonderbund.

14952.q: What did the cantons of the Sonderbund mainly have in common?
a: They were all on Lake Geneva.
14952.e: The Sonderbund cantons were strongly Catholic and wanted to protect their old order and the rights of the Church.
14952.m: The Sonderbund was an alliance of Catholic conservative cantons.

14953.q: Who were the political opponents of the Sonderbund?
14953.e: The Liberals and Radicals (later the Free Democrats) wanted a stronger federal state and were in power in most cantons.
14953.m: Liberals and Radicals fought against the Sonderbund.

14954.q: Which dispute stirred up strong feelings in 1841 and helped lead to the Sonderbund?
a: The closing of the monasteries in Aargau
The building of the Gotthard Tunnel
The founding of ETH in Zurich
14954.e: In 1841 the canton of Aargau closed its monasteries. For the Catholic cantons this was an attack on their religion.
14954.m: The Aargau monastery dispute sharpened the conflict before the Sonderbund.

14955.q: Which religious order did Lucerne bring to its higher schools in 1844, angering the Liberals?
14955.e: The Liberals saw the appointment of the Jesuits in Lucerne as a provocation, and it led to raids by volunteer corps against Lucerne.
14955.m: Bringing the Jesuits to Lucerne greatly inflamed the dispute.

14956.q: What were the armed groups of Liberals called that marched against Lucerne in 1844 and 1845?
14956.e: Freischaren were volunteer, unofficial troops of Liberals and Radicals. Their attacks on Lucerne failed.
14956.m: The Freischaren raids on Lucerne failed in 1844 and 1845.

14957.q: What did the Sonderbund cantons want to prevent?
14957.e: The Sonderbund cantons wanted to keep their independence and the rights of the Church. They rejected a strong federal state.
14957.m: The Sonderbund was against a strong federal state.

14958.q: Why did the majority of the Diet consider the Sonderbund not allowed?
a: It broke the Federal Treaty of 1815.
It had no name of its own.
14958.e: The Federal Treaty of 1815 banned alliances between cantons that harmed the Confederation or other cantons. That is why the majority demanded that it be dissolved.
14958.m: The majority of the Diet saw the Sonderbund as a breach of the Federal Treaty.

14959.q: What did the majority of the Diet demand of the Sonderbund in 1847?
14959.e: After Geneva and St Gallen had become liberal, the Diet decided in July 1847 that the Sonderbund must be dissolved.
14959.m: In 1847 the Diet demanded that the Sonderbund be dissolved.

14960.q: Who came up with the name “Sonderbund” (separate alliance)?
14960.e: The members called their alliance a Protective Union. The Liberals called it the Sonderbund, and this name stuck.
14960.m: The name Sonderbund came from its opponents.

14961.q: In which year did the Sonderbund War take place?
14961.e: The Sonderbund War lasted from 3 to 29 November 1847.
14961.m: The Sonderbund War took place in November 1847.

14962.q: Who was general of the Confederate troops in the Sonderbund War?
14962.e: Guillaume-Henri Dufour from Geneva led the troops of the Diet. Henri Guisan was general in the Second World War.
14962.m: General Dufour led the Confederate army in the Sonderbund War.

14964.q: Which side won the Sonderbund War?
a: The Confederate troops of the Diet
Nobody, it ended in a draw
14964.e: The Confederate army was much larger and defeated the Sonderbund cantons within a few weeks.
14964.m: The troops of the Diet defeated the Sonderbund.

14965.q: Roughly how big was the Confederate army in the Sonderbund War?
14965.e: The Diet called up around 99,000 soldiers, the Sonderbund around 79,000.
14965.m: The Confederate army had almost 100,000 soldiers.

14967.q: Why did capturing Lucerne matter so much in the Sonderbund War?
a: Lucerne was the largest city in Europe
14967.e: Lucerne led the Sonderbund. Once Lucerne had been occupied on 24 November 1847, the Sonderbund had practically lost.
14967.m: With Lucerne the most important canton of the Sonderbund fell.

14968.q: Which city was occupied by the Confederate troops on 24 November 1847?
14968.e: After the defeats of 23 November, Lucerne, the leading canton of the Sonderbund, surrendered and troops occupied it.
14968.m: Once Lucerne had been occupied, the Sonderbund had practically lost.

14969.q: Which canton was the last to surrender, on 29 November 1847?
14969.e: Valais surrendered as the last Sonderbund canton. That ended the war.
14969.m: Valais surrendered last of all the Sonderbund cantons.

14970.q: What is the commander of the Confederate troops in the Sonderbund War especially known for?
a: He ordered prisoners and wounded to be treated humanely.
He changed sides to the Sonderbund.
He fought the war with aeroplanes.
14970.e: Dufour wanted a short war with as few victims as possible and demanded that the wounded, prisoners and civilians be spared.
14970.m: The Confederate general fought the war as gently as possible.

14971.q: Roughly how many deaths did the Sonderbund War cause?
14971.e: The figures vary: according to official numbers, around 150 people died and around 400 were wounded. Compared with other wars, the losses were small.
14971.m: The Sonderbund War caused relatively few deaths.

14972.q: What did the Diet decide on 4 November 1847?
a: To dissolve the Sonderbund by force
To make Bern the federal city
14972.e: After negotiations had failed, the Diet decided on 4 November 1847 to defeat the Sonderbund militarily.
14972.m: On 4 November 1847 the Diet decided on war against the Sonderbund.

14973.q: Why did the Sonderbund War end so quickly?
a: The Confederate army was larger and well led
14973.e: General Dufour led a larger army and acted quickly and to a plan. So the Sonderbund cantons were defeated within a few weeks.
14973.m: The superior Confederate army ended the war quickly.

14974.q: On which day did the Diet declare the new Federal Constitution accepted?
14974.e: On 12 September 1848 the Diet declared the Federal Constitution accepted. This day is seen as the birthday of the federal state.
14974.m: The first Federal Constitution was accepted on 12 September 1848.

14975.q: Which agreement was replaced by the Federal Constitution of 1848?
14975.e: The Federal Treaty of 1815 was a loose treaty between cantons. The Constitution of 1848 took its place.
14975.m: The Constitution of 1848 replaced the Federal Treaty of 1815.

14977.q: Which of these cantons rejected the Federal Constitution of 1848?
14977.e: It was rejected mainly by former Sonderbund cantons such as Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Zug and Valais, plus Ticino and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
14977.m: Uri was one of the cantons that rejected the Constitution in 1848.

14978.q: Which country was the model for Switzerland’s two-chamber parliament?
14978.e: The two-chamber system, with a chamber of the people and a chamber of the member states, was based on the US Constitution. The chamber of the cantons corresponds to the Senate.
14978.m: The Swiss two-chamber system follows the example of the USA.

14979.q: What was abolished inside Switzerland by the Federal Constitution of 1848?
14979.e: Before, cantons collected customs duties at their borders. From 1848 there was a single economic area, and only the Confederation charged duties at the national border.
14979.m: Since 1848 there have been no customs duties between the cantons.

14980.q: Who was allowed to vote at federal level under the Constitution of 1848?
14980.e: In 1848 only men had the right to vote. Women only got it at federal level more than 120 years later.
14980.m: The Constitution of 1848 gave the vote only to men.

14981.q: Who did NOT at first have the freedom to settle anywhere in Switzerland under the Constitution of 1848?
14981.e: In 1848 the freedom of settlement applied only to Christian Swiss. Jews were given equal rights only later.
14981.m: The freedom of settlement of 1848 at first excluded Jews.

14982.q: Which cantons faced each other in the Sonderbund War before the Constitution of 1848?
14982.e: The liberal cantons wanted a stronger Confederation. The Catholic conservative cantons joined together in the Sonderbund and lost in 1847.
14982.m: In the Sonderbund War liberal cantons fought Catholic conservative cantons.

14983.q: What was the Confederation responsible for from 1848, instead of the cantons?
14983.e: In 1848 the Confederation was given only a few tasks, such as coinage, measures and weights, and foreign policy. Schools, police and criminal law stayed with the cantons.
14983.m: Since 1848 the Confederation has regulated coins, measures and weights, among other things.

14985.q: Since when has Switzerland’s current Federal Constitution been in force?
14985.e: The people and the cantons accepted the new Federal Constitution on 18 April 1999. It came into force on 1 January 2000.
14985.m: The current Federal Constitution has been in force since 2000.

14986.q: Which new government did the Federal Constitution of 1848 create?
14986.e: With the Constitution of 1848 Switzerland got a national government, the Federal Council. At that time it was elected for three years.
14986.m: Since 1848 the Federal Council has governed Switzerland.

14987.q: What is the form of state that Switzerland got in 1848 called?
14987.e: Before 1848 Switzerland was a loose confederation of states. From 1848 it was a federal state with a common government and a common parliament.
14987.m: Since 1848 Switzerland has been a federal state.

14988.q: What is the most important difference between a confederation of states and a federal state?
a: A federal state has a common government and a common parliament.
A confederation of states always has a king.
A federal state no longer has member states.
A confederation of states always has only one language.
14988.e: In a confederation of states the members stay largely independent. In a federal state there is also a central state with its own authorities.
14988.m: A federal state has its own common authorities.

14989.q: Which city did the Federal Assembly choose on 28 November 1848 as the seat of the federal authorities?
14989.e: Bern won the most votes in both chambers in the very first round. Since then Bern has been the seat of the Federal Council and Parliament.
14989.m: Bern has been the seat of the Federal Council and Parliament since 1848.

14990.q: Why is Bern called the “federal city” rather than the “capital”?
a: Because no capital is set down in law
Because Bern is the largest city
Because Bern is in the canton of Zurich
Because the king lives in Bern
14990.e: Legally, Switzerland has no capital. Bern is the seat of the federal authorities and is therefore called the federal city.
14990.m: Bern is the federal city of Switzerland.

14991.q: Which city was Bern’s strongest rival for the federal seat in 1848?
14991.e: In the National Council, Bern received 58 votes, Zurich 35 and Lucerne 6. Zurich also came second in the Council of States.
14991.m: Zurich lost to Bern in the race for the federal seat in 1848.

14992.q: Which important university did Zurich receive, in a way as compensation for not becoming the federal seat?
14992.e: Zurich became the home of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH). Lausanne later received the Federal Supreme Court.
14992.m: Zurich received ETH as the federal university.

14993.q: In which year was the franc introduced as the single currency for all of Switzerland?
14993.e: With the Coinage Act of 7 May 1850 the Swiss franc became the common currency. Before that the cantons had many coins of their own.
14993.m: Since 1850 people have paid with francs throughout Switzerland.

14994.q: Which currency served as the model for the Swiss franc in 1850?
14994.e: The new franc followed the French silver franc. One franc has 100 centimes (Rappen).
14994.m: The Swiss franc was modelled on the French franc.

14995.q: How many cantons did Switzerland have when the federal state was founded in 1848?
14995.e: In 1848 there were 22 cantons, some of them split into half-cantons. Today Switzerland has 26 cantons.
14995.m: When the federal state was founded there were 22 cantons.

14996.q: Which canton was the youngest, joining only in 1979?
14996.e: The canton of Jura was created in 1979 by splitting off from the canton of Bern. It is the youngest canton in Switzerland.
14996.m: Jura has been the youngest canton since 1979.

14997.q: Which party had won the Sonderbund War and then governed the young federal state alone for decades?
14997.e: The Free Democrats (today the FDP) provided all members of the Federal Council until 1891. Only then did a Catholic conservative join.
14997.m: The Free Democrats governed the federal state alone in its first decades.

14998.q: In which year was 1 August celebrated as the national day for the first time?
14998.e: In 1891 people celebrated the 600th anniversary of the Confederation on 1 August. It has been celebrated every year since 1899, and since a popular vote in 1993 it has been a public holiday.
14998.m: 1 August was first celebrated as the national day in 1891.

14999.q: How many members does the Federal Council have?
14999.e: Since 1848 the Federal Council has had seven members with equal rights.
14999.m: The Federal Council has seven members.

15000.q: Who elects the members of the Federal Council?
a: The people at the ballot box
15000.e: The National Council and the Council of States elect the Federal Council together as the United Federal Assembly.

15001.q: For how many years is the Federal Council elected today?
15001.e: The members of the Federal Council are elected for four years, each time after the National Council elections.
15001.m: The Federal Council is elected for four years.

15002.q: How long is the term of office of the President of the Confederation?
15002.e: The presidency changes every year. The president chairs the meetings but is only first among equals.
15002.m: The presidency of the Confederation changes every year.

15003.q: What does the principle of collegiality in the Federal Council mean?
a: The Federal Council decides together and stands by its decisions together.
The people decide at every meeting.
15003.e: The members of the Federal Council support decisions together, even if they disagreed in private.
15003.m: The Federal Council stands by its decisions together.

15004.q: What does each member of the Federal Council lead?
15004.e: Each member of the Federal Council heads a department, for example the Department of Defence. The number of departments has stayed the same since 1848.
15004.m: Each member of the Federal Council heads a department.

15005.q: When was the first Federal Council elected?
15005.e: The newly elected Federal Assembly elected the first seven Federal Councillors on 16 November 1848.
15005.m: The first Federal Council was elected in November 1848.

15006.q: Who chairs the meetings of the Federal Council?
a: The President of the National Council
The President of the Federal Supreme Court
15006.e: The presidency changes every year. The president chairs the meetings. The first President of the Confederation, in 1848, was Jonas Furrer.
15006.m: The President of the Confederation chairs the Federal Council’s meetings.

15007.q: Which language region did Stefano Franscini represent in the first Federal Council of 1848?
15007.e: Stefano Franscini came from Ticino. He represented Italian-speaking Switzerland in the first Federal Council.
15007.m: Stefano Franscini was the first Federal Councillor from Ticino.

15008.q: Who was elected to the Federal Council in 1984 as the first woman?
15008.e: Elisabeth Kopp became a member on 2 October 1984. She was the first woman in the national government.
15008.m: In 1984 Elisabeth Kopp became the first woman Federal Councillor.

15009.q: What is the distribution of seats in the Federal Council that applied from 1959 called?
15009.e: From 1959 the FDP, CVP and SP each got two seats and the SVP one seat. In 2003 one CVP seat went to the SVP.
15009.m: From 1959 the magic formula shared the Federal Council seats among four parties.

15010.q: Which party got a seat in the Federal Council for the first time in 1943, with Ernst Nobs?
15010.e: Ernst Nobs was elected to the Federal Council on 15 December 1943 as the first Social Democrat.
15010.m: Ernst Nobs was the first SP Federal Councillor in 1943.

15011.q: What does concordance mean in Swiss politics?
a: As many major parties as possible take part in government.
The Federal Council is chosen by lot.
15011.e: Concordance is an unwritten principle: the big parties should all be represented together in the Federal Council.
15011.m: Concordance means that the big parties govern together.

15012.q: Who does the National Council represent first and foremost?
15012.e: The National Council is the chamber of the people. Its seats are shared out among the cantons according to population.
15012.m: The National Council represents the people.

15013.q: How are the 200 National Council seats shared out among the cantons?
a: Each canton gets the same number
According to the age of the canton
15013.e: Cantons with more people get more seats. But every canton is entitled to at least one seat.
15013.m: National Council seats depend on the population of the cantons.

15014.q: Which canton has the most seats in the National Council?
15014.e: Zurich is the canton with the largest population and had 36 seats in the 2023 elections.
15014.m: Zurich has the most members of the National Council.

15015.q: What is the minimum number of seats each canton has in the National Council?
15015.e: Even very small cantons such as Uri or Appenzell Innerrhoden have at least one seat in the National Council.
15015.m: Every canton has at least one seat in the National Council.

15016.q: How often is the National Council elected?
15016.e: The National Council is elected by the people every four years in October, most recently in October 2023.
15016.m: The National Council is elected every four years.

15017.q: Which voting system has been used to elect the National Council since 1919?
15017.e: Since 1919 the seats have been shared out in proportion to the parties’ votes. As a result the Free Democrats lost their absolute majority.
15017.m: Since 1919 the National Council has been elected by proportional representation.

15018.q: How many members does the National Council have today?
15018.e: The National Council has 200 members. Together with the 46 members of the Council of States, that makes 246 members of parliament.

15019.q: How many women were elected in 1971 as the first women members of the National Council?
15019.e: In the first elections with women’s suffrage in 1971, eleven women entered the National Council.
15019.m: In 1971 the first eleven women were elected to the National Council.

15020.q: What does each canton form in the National Council elections?
15020.e: In the National Council elections each canton is one constituency. The parties put up lists in each canton.
15020.m: Each canton is one constituency in National Council elections.

15021.q: How many times a year do the regular sessions of Parliament take place?
15021.e: Parliament meets four times a year for sessions of three weeks each: in spring, summer, autumn and winter.
15021.m: Parliament meets four times a year in sessions.

15022.q: What is another name for the National Council?
15022.e: Because it is much larger than the Council of States, with 200 members, the National Council is also called the Large Chamber.
15022.m: The National Council is also called the Large Chamber.

15023.q: Who does the Council of States represent?
15023.e: The Council of States is the chamber of the cantons. Each canton has almost the same weight, whatever its size.
15023.m: The Council of States represents the cantons.

15024.q: How many members of the Council of States does a canton like Zurich or Uri have?
15024.e: In the Council of States population does not count: big Zurich and little Uri each have two seats.
15024.m: Large and small cantons have the same number of seats in the Council of States.

15025.q: Which cantons have only one seat in the Council of States?
a: The former half-cantons such as Basel-Stadt
The border cantons such as Geneva
The mountain cantons such as the Grisons
The lake cantons such as Zug
15025.e: Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each have one seat in the Council of States.
15025.m: The six former half-cantons each have one seat in the Council of States.

15026.q: What is the assembly called when the National Council and the Council of States meet together?
15026.e: Together, the members of the National Council and the Council of States form the United Federal Assembly. It elects the Federal Council, for example.
15026.m: The United Federal Assembly is made up of both chambers.

15027.q: How many members does the United Federal Assembly have?
15027.e: 200 members of the National Council and 46 of the Council of States add up to 246.
15027.m: The United Federal Assembly has 246 members.

15028.q: Who decides how the members of the Council of States are elected?
15028.e: The Federal Constitution leaves the voting procedure to the cantons. Today the people elect the members of the Council of States in all cantons.
15028.m: Each canton decides for itself how it elects its members of the Council of States.

15029.q: Who elects the members of the Council of States in the cantons today?
15029.e: In the past, the cantonal parliaments elected the members of the Council of States in some cantons. Today the people elect them everywhere.
15029.m: Members of the Council of States are elected by the people today.

15030.q: What rights does the Council of States have compared with the National Council?
15030.e: Both chambers have equal rights. A law is only passed if both the National Council and the Council of States agree.
15030.m: The National Council and the Council of States have equal rights.

15031.q: What happens to a new law if the National Council says yes but the Council of States says no?
a: It only applies in large cantons
15031.e: A law needs the approval of both councils. If they still cannot agree after several rounds of debate, the law has failed.
15031.m: A law needs a yes from both the National Council and the Council of States.

15032.q: In which year could women be elected to the Council of States for the first time?
15032.e: In 1971 women in Switzerland got the right to vote and stand for election at federal level. In the same year the first woman was elected to the Council of States.
15032.m: Since 1971 women can be elected to the Council of States.

15033.q: What is another name for the Council of States?
15033.e: With 46 members, the Council of States is much smaller than the National Council and is therefore called the Small Chamber.
15033.m: The Council of States is also called the Small Chamber.

15034.q: Within what time limit must the signatures for an optional referendum be collected?
15034.e: After a law is published, there are 100 days left for the referendum.

15035.q: What is the aim of a popular initiative?
a: To propose a change to the Federal Constitution
To stop a law passed by Parliament afterwards
15035.e: With a popular initiative, citizens can demand an addition to or change in the Federal Constitution. With a referendum, on the other hand, laws are stopped.
15035.m: With a popular initiative the people propose a change to the constitution.

15036.q: What is the “double majority” in votes on the constitution?
a: A majority of the people and a majority of the cantons
A majority in the National Council and in the Federal Council
Two votes on the same day
15036.e: A change to the constitution is only accepted if both the majority of voters (popular majority) and the majority of the cantons (cantonal majority) agree.
15036.m: Changes to the constitution need the popular majority and the cantonal majority.

15037.q: When must there always be a popular vote in Switzerland (mandatory referendum)?
a: For every change to the Federal Constitution
15037.e: Every change to the Federal Constitution must be put to the people and the cantons. That is why this referendum is called mandatory.
15037.m: Changes to the constitution always go to the people.

15038.q: How often do national votes usually take place in Switzerland?
15038.e: Each year the Confederation usually sets four voting Sundays. Several proposals can be voted on on one Sunday.
15038.m: National votes usually take place four times a year.

15040.q: When did Swiss men approve votes for women at federal level?
15040.e: On 7 February 1971 men approved votes for women with around 66 per cent voting yes. A first attempt had failed in 1959.
15040.m: Since 1971 women in Switzerland have been able to vote and be elected at federal level.

15041.q: Which canton had to be forced by the Federal Supreme Court in 1990 to give women the vote?
15041.e: The Landsgemeinde of Appenzell Innerrhoden still rejected votes for women in April 1990. In November 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that this was against the constitution.
15041.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to give women the vote, in 1990.

15042.q: From what age can you vote and stand for election at federal level in Switzerland?
15042.e: Since 1991 the voting age at federal level has been 18; before that it was 20.
15042.m: At federal level you can vote from the age of 18.

15043.q: In which two cantons is there still a Landsgemeinde today?
15043.e: At the Landsgemeinde, voters gather in the open air and vote by raising their hands. Today this only happens in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
15043.m: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden still hold a Landsgemeinde.

15044.q: What is heated in a steam engine to make steam?
15044.e: In the boiler, water is heated so much that it turns into steam. The steam pushes a piston back and forth. Thomas Newcomen built the first usable steam engine in 1712.
15044.m: In a steam engine, hot steam drives a piston.

15045.q: What were Newcomen’s first steam engines mainly used for?
15045.e: Water kept flooding into the coal mines. Newcomen’s engine pumped this water out so the miners could dig deeper.
15045.m: The first steam engines pumped water out of mines.

15046.q: Who improved the steam engine so that it needed much less coal?
15046.e: James Watt improved the steam engine and patented it in 1769. His engine used much less coal than Newcomen’s old one.
15046.m: James Watt made the steam engine more economical.

15047.q: Which important improvement did James Watt make to the steam engine?
15047.e: Watt let the steam cool in a separate container, the condenser. This kept the cylinder hot, and the engine wasted much less energy.
15047.m: Thanks to James Watt’s separate condenser, the steam engine saved a lot of coal.

15048.q: Which fuel was mainly burned in the steam engines of industrialisation?
15048.e: Under the boiler of a steam engine, hard coal usually burned. That is why coal regions like those in England or the Ruhr became centres of industry.
15048.m: Steam engines were mainly heated with coal.

15049.q: Which unit of power is named after James Watt?
15049.e: In honour of James Watt, the unit of power is called the “watt”. Today you can find it, for example, on every light bulb or hairdryer.
15049.m: The unit watt is named after the inventor James Watt.

15050.q: Which unit of power did James Watt introduce to compare his engines with working animals?
15050.e: Watt wanted to show how many horses his engine could replace. So he converted its power into horsepower (hp).
15050.m: Horsepower (hp) showed how many horses an engine could replace.

15051.q: Why was the steam engine so important for factories?
a: Factories no longer had to be by a river.
15051.e: Before, water wheels drove the machines, so factories were by rivers. With the steam engine, factories could be built anywhere, for example in towns.
15051.m: With the steam engine, factories were no longer tied to rivers.

15052.q: In which country did industrialisation begin in the second half of the 18th century?
15052.e: Great Britain had plenty of coal and iron, money from traders and many inventors. That is why the Industrial Revolution began there.

15053.q: What is the great change called in which machines increasingly replaced handwork?
15053.e: From about 1750, machines, factories and steam power greatly changed people’s work and lives. This change is called the Industrial Revolution.
15053.m: The Industrial Revolution changed work and life through machines.

15054.q: Which new means of transport was driven by a steam engine in the 19th century?
15054.e: A locomotive is a steam engine on wheels. It pulled railway carriages over long distances.
15054.m: The steam locomotive brought steam power onto the rails.

15055.q: What drove the first steamships forward?
15055.e: The steam engine turned large paddle wheels at the side or the back. In 1807 Robert Fulton made the steamship a success with the “Clermont”.
15055.m: Early steamships were driven by paddle wheels.

15056.q: Which spinning machine did James Hargreaves invent in 1764?
15056.e: With the spinning jenny one person could spin several threads at once. This made spinning much faster.
15056.m: The spinning jenny of 1764 spun several threads at once.

15057.q: In which branch of industry did the first factories of industrialisation appear?
15057.e: The first factories spun and wove cotton. Yarn and cloth could be made much faster with machines than by hand.
15057.m: The first factories made yarn and cloth.

15058.q: What changed when power looms came in?
a: Cloth could be woven much faster.
Cloth was only made of paper.
15058.e: Power looms were driven by machines. So much more cloth was made in a short time than by hand, and many hand weavers lost their work.
15058.m: Power looms made weaving much faster.

15059.q: What does “division of labour” mean in a factory?
a: Each worker does only one particular step of the work.
Each worker makes a whole product alone.
The workers share their wages equally.
The workers take turns working at home.
15059.e: In the factory, production was split into many small steps. Each worker repeated the same task over and over, which made production faster.
15059.m: With division of labour, each person does only one small step.

15060.q: What is the way of working before factories called, in which families spun and wove at home for a merchant?
15060.e: Many families, including in the Zurich Oberland, spun and wove in their own living rooms. A merchant brought the raw material and collected the finished goods.
15060.m: Before factories, many families worked at home.

15061.q: What were the workers in England called who destroyed machines around 1811 and 1812 because they feared for their jobs?
15061.e: The machine breakers, also called Luddites in England, smashed weaving machines. They feared that the machines would take away their work and wages.
15061.m: Machine breakers destroyed machines because they feared for their jobs.

15062.q: How long did factory workers often work each day at the beginning of industrialisation?
15062.e: At first there were hardly any laws to protect workers. Working days of 12 to 16 hours, Saturdays included, were normal.
15062.m: In the past factory workers often worked 12 to 16 hours a day.

15063.q: What is the growth of towns called, as many people moved from the countryside to the factory towns?
15063.e: Factories needed many workers, so people moved from the countryside to the towns. The towns grew very quickly, often with cramped and dirty housing areas.
15063.m: Industrialisation made the towns grow strongly.

15064.q: Who introduced the assembly line in car production in 1913?
15064.e: From 1913 Henry Ford had his Model T built on an assembly line. This made cars much faster and cheaper to produce.
15064.m: Henry Ford introduced the assembly line in car production in 1913.

15065.q: Which English city became the centre of the textile industry because of its many cotton mills?
15065.e: In the 19th century Manchester had countless cotton mills. The city became the symbol of industrialisation.
15065.m: Manchester was the centre of the English cotton industry.

15066.q: What did a set of factory rules regulate in the 19th century?
a: The workers’ hours, duties and punishments
The prices of goods in shops
The election of the factory owner
15066.e: The factory rules contained strict rules, for example about when you had to turn up. Anyone who came late or chatted often had money taken off their wages.
15066.m: The factory rules set strict rules for the workers.

15067.q: Why were many early spinning mills by rivers?
a: The yarn had to float in the river.
15067.e: The first large spinning machines were driven by water power. That is why spinning mills were built by rivers, in Switzerland too, for example in the Zurich Oberland.
15067.m: Early spinning mills used water power.

15068.q: In which country did the first public railway with steam locomotives run in 1825?
15068.e: The Stockton and Darlington Railway in England opened in 1825. It mainly carried coal from the mines to the ports.
15068.m: The first public steam railway ran in England in 1825.

15069.q: Roughly what was the top speed of the famous locomotive “Rocket” of 1829?
15069.e: Robert Stephenson’s “Rocket” reached almost 50 kilometres per hour. At that time that was faster than any horse-drawn coach.
15069.m: The “Rocket” was faster than any coach.

15070.q: What was new when the railway from Liverpool to Manchester opened in 1830?
a: It was meant for passengers and ran to a timetable.
15070.e: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830. It carried passengers and goods to a fixed timetable and became a model for many railways.
15070.m: The Liverpool to Manchester railway became a model in 1830.

15071.q: Which engineer is known as the “Father of Railways” and built locomotives with his son Robert?
15071.e: George Stephenson built locomotives and railway lines in England. Together with his son Robert he strongly shaped early railway building.
15071.m: George Stephenson is known as the “Father of Railways”.

15072.q: What is the distance between the two rails of a track called?
15072.e: The gauge is the distance between the rails. The most common gauge in the world is standard gauge at 1,435 millimetres, which is also used by SBB, the Swiss Federal Railways.
15072.m: The distance between the rails is called the gauge.

15073.q: Which country did the locomotive “Adler” of the first German railway in 1835 come from?
15073.e: England was far ahead in building railways. So a locomotive from England was bought for the first German railway from Nuremberg to Fürth.
15073.m: The first locomotives in Germany came from England.

15074.q: How did the railway change trade in the 19th century?
a: Goods could be transported faster and more cheaply.
Goods could only be carried by horses.
Goods became much dearer and slower.
15074.e: By rail, coal, grain and factory goods could be moved quickly in large amounts. This lowered prices and helped industry.
15074.m: The railway made transporting goods faster and cheaper.

15075.q: What was the name of the first railway line that lay entirely on Swiss soil?
15075.e: The Swiss Northern Railway linked Zurich with Baden. People call it the “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn” (Spanish Roll Railway), after a pastry from Baden.
15075.m: The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn was the first railway entirely on Swiss soil.

15076.q: In which year did the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn from Zurich to Baden open?
15076.e: The line was officially opened on 7 August 1847. It was about 23 kilometres long.
15076.m: From 1847 the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn ran from Zurich to Baden.

15077.q: Which railway line already reached Swiss soil in 1844?
a: The railway from Strasbourg to Basel
The railway from Milan to Lugano
The railway from Geneva to Lausanne
The railway from Vienna to St Gallen
15077.e: In 1844 the Alsace railway linked Strasbourg with Basel. It was the first railway to reach Swiss territory, but lay mostly in France.
15077.m: As early as 1844 a railway ran from Strasbourg to Basel.

15078.q: Where does the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn from Zurich to Baden get its name from?
15078.e: The “Spanische Brötli” (Spanish rolls) were a fine pastry from Baden. Thanks to the railway they arrived in Zurich still fresh for breakfast.
15078.m: The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn is named after a pastry from Baden.

15079.q: In which year were the Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) founded?
15079.e: Before, Swiss railways belonged to private companies. The SBB were created in 1902, when the Confederation took over the large private railways.

15080.q: Which important source of energy did Swiss factories use, because Switzerland has hardly any coal?
15080.e: Switzerland has hardly any coal of its own, but many rivers and streams. That is why many spinning mills stood by rivers and used water wheels and turbines.
15080.m: Swiss factories mainly used water power.

15081.q: Which industry was the most important in Switzerland at the beginning of industrialisation?
15081.e: Spinning mills, weaving mills and embroidery works employed a great many people in Switzerland. Centres included Zurich, the Zurich Oberland, Glarus and eastern Switzerland.
15081.m: In Switzerland industrialisation began with the textile industry.

15082.q: What did Swiss engineering works such as Escher Wyss or Sulzer make in the 19th century?
15082.e: Many engineering works started as spinning mills and first built their own textile machines. Later they made turbines, steam engines and steamships.
15082.m: In Switzerland spinning mills grew into engineering works.

15083.q: What happened in 1832 in the Uster fire in the Zurich Oberland?
a: Home weavers set fire to a mechanical weaving mill.
Lightning destroyed the church in Uster.
The town of Uster burned down in a war.
A steam locomotive exploded in the station.
15083.e: On 22 November 1832 home workers set fire to the Corrodi & Pfister spinning and weaving mill in Oberuster. They feared that the weaving machines would take away their work.
15083.m: In the Uster fire of 1832, home weavers destroyed a factory out of fear for their jobs.

15084.q: Which Zurich politician and businessman founded railways and a major bank and supported ETH?
15084.e: Alfred Escher was one of the most powerful men in Switzerland in the 19th century. He worked for railways, a big bank and the Gotthard Railway.
15084.m: Alfred Escher was an important pioneer of modern Switzerland.

15085.q: In which year did the Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) in Zurich begin teaching?
15085.e: ETH began in 1855 as the “Polytechnikum”. It trained engineers, whom Switzerland urgently needed for railways and factories.

15086.q: Which industry is the Jura Arc in Switzerland especially known for?
15086.e: In the Jura, for example in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle or Biel, many watch factories were set up. Swiss watches were sold all over the world.
15086.m: The Jura Arc is a centre of the Swiss watch industry.

15087.q: In which Swiss city did a large chemical industry grow up in the 19th century, starting with dyes?
15087.e: In Basel, companies first made dyes for the textile industry. This later developed into the large pharmaceutical industry.
15087.m: Basel became the centre of Swiss chemistry.

15088.q: Which product was eastern Switzerland around St Gallen world-famous for in the 19th century?
15088.e: St Gallen embroidery was exported to many countries. For a time embroidery was one of Switzerland’s most important exports.
15088.m: St Gallen was world-famous for its embroidery.

15089.q: Which bank did Alfred Escher found in 1856 to finance railway building?
15089.e: Building railways was expensive and needed a lot of money. So in 1856 Alfred Escher founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, which later became Credit Suisse.
15089.m: Alfred Escher founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt in 1856.

15090.q: What did the first mechanical spinning mills in Switzerland make?
15090.e: In spinning mills, machines twisted cotton into yarn. One of the first successful ones was the Hard spinning mill near Winterthur around 1802.
15090.m: Spinning mills used machines to make yarn from cotton.

15091.q: Why did many people emigrate from Switzerland to America in the 19th century?
a: Because of poverty and lack of work
Because of a war in Switzerland
Because there was no work in America
15091.e: Many home workers lost their income because of the machines, and there were bad harvests. So many looked for a better life overseas.
15091.m: Poverty drove many Swiss to emigrate in the 19th century.

15092.q: In which year did the Gotthard Railway open in full?
15092.e: On 1 June 1882 the whole Gotthard Railway went into service. It linked German-speaking Switzerland directly with Ticino and Italy.

15093.q: Roughly how long is the old Gotthard railway tunnel from Göschenen to Airolo?
15093.e: The summit tunnel is about 15 kilometres long. When it opened, it was the longest railway tunnel in the world.
15093.m: The old Gotthard tunnel is about 15 kilometres long.

15094.q: When did the tunnel builders from the north and south meet in the breakthrough of the Gotthard tunnel?
15094.e: After more than seven years of work, the two tunnels met inside the mountain on 29 February 1880. They were only very slightly out of line.
15094.m: The breakthrough in the Gotthard tunnel happened in 1880.

15095.q: Which builder from Geneva led the building of the Gotthard tunnel but did not live to see the breakthrough?
15095.e: Louis Favre died of heart failure in the tunnel on 19 July 1879. He did not live to see the breakthrough half a year later.
15095.m: Louis Favre built the Gotthard tunnel and died in 1879 before the breakthrough.

15096.q: Which country did most of the workers building the Gotthard tunnel come from?
15096.e: Most of the miners came from poor areas in Piedmont and Lombardy. They worked in very hard and dangerous conditions.
15096.m: The Gotthard tunnel was built mainly by Italian workers.

15097.q: Roughly how many workers died building the Gotthard tunnel?
15097.e: During the building work 199 workers died, many from wagons, falling rocks or explosives. Many more died later of illness and injuries.
15097.m: About 200 workers died building the Gotthard tunnel.

15098.q: What happened during the strike of the tunnel workers in Göschenen in 1875?
a: Armed men fired into the crowd and four workers died.
The workers immediately got double pay.
Building the tunnel was stopped for ever.
The workers took over running the building work.
15098.e: On 27 July 1875 the workers went on strike for more pay and better conditions. A police unit from Altdorf fired into the crowd, and four Italian workers died.
15098.m: During the strike in Göschenen in 1875 four workers were shot dead.

15099.q: What is the village of Wassen on the Gotthard Railway known for?
a: From the train you see its church three times from different heights.
It has the highest railway station in Europe.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel starts there.
The first locomotive was built there.
15099.e: Near Wassen the railway climbs the slope with loops and spiral tunnels. The church on a rocky ledge can be seen from all three levels of the line.
15099.m: At Wassen you see the church three times thanks to spiral tunnels.

15100.q: Why was the Gotthard Railway switched to electric power?
a: Coal was scarce in the First World War.
15100.e: Switzerland had to buy coal from abroad, and during the war it was scarce and expensive. Electricity from water power, on the other hand, was available in the country itself.
15100.m: The Gotthard Railway runs on electricity from water power.

15101.q: How long is the Gotthard Base Tunnel, which opened in 2016?
15101.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long and opened on 1 June 2016. It is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
15101.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long.

15102.q: Which neighbouring countries helped to pay for building the Gotthard Railway?
15102.e: The Gotthard Railway was also important for trade between north and south. That is why Italy and Germany shared the costs.
15102.m: Italy and Germany helped pay for the Gotthard Railway.

15103.q: What was Alfred Escher’s role in the Gotthard Railway?
a: He was president of the Gotthard Railway Company.
He dug the tunnel as a miner.
15103.e: Alfred Escher campaigned hard for the Gotthard line and led the Gotthard Railway Company. Because of a financial crisis he resigned in 1879.
15103.m: Alfred Escher led the Gotthard Railway Company.

15104.q: When did work start on the Gotthard railway tunnel?
15104.e: In autumn 1872 work began at both tunnel entrances, in Göschenen and Airolo. After about seven and a half years the two sides broke through.
15104.m: Work on the Gotthard Tunnel began in 1872.

15105.q: In which workplaces did children especially often have to work during industrialisation?
15105.e: In textile factories children tied broken threads back together. In mines they crawled through narrow tunnels because they were small.
15105.m: Children often worked in spinning mills and mines.

15106.q: Why did factory owners like to employ children?
a: Children were paid much lower wages.
15106.e: Children earned only a fraction of an adult’s wage. Even so, many poor families needed their earnings to survive.
15106.m: Child labour was cheap for factory owners.

15107.q: Why were children particularly suited to certain jobs in mines?
a: They were small and could fit through narrow tunnels.
They could see better in the dark.
They did not need air to breathe.
15107.e: Many passages in the coal mines were very low. Small children pulled carts there or opened ventilation doors, often for hours in the dark.
15107.m: Small children often had to work in narrow mine tunnels.

15108.q: Which country was the first to appoint state factory inspectors to protect children, with a Factory Act in 1833?
15108.e: The British Factory Act of 1833 banned children under 9 from working in textile factories and limited the working hours of older ones. For the first time, paid inspectors checked that the rules were followed.
15108.m: Great Britain appointed factory inspectors to protect children in 1833.

15109.q: From what age were children allowed to work in factories in Switzerland under the Factory Act of 1877?
15109.e: The federal Factory Act banned factory work for children under 14. This gave them more time for school.
15109.m: From 1877, children under 14 were not allowed to work in Swiss factories.

15110.q: What was the longest a working day in a factory could last under the Swiss Factory Act of 1877?
15110.e: The Factory Act introduced the 11-hour day. There were also rules against night and Sunday work.
15110.m: The Factory Act of 1877 limited the working day to 11 hours.

15111.q: How was the federal Factory Act of 1877 introduced?
a: The people narrowly approved it in a vote.
A king ordered it without a vote.
The factory owners wrote it on their own.
15111.e: On 21 October 1877 Swiss men voted on the law. It was passed with only 51.5 per cent voting yes.
15111.m: The people narrowly approved the Factory Act in 1877.

15112.q: Under the Swiss Factory Act of 1877, who checked that the rules were being followed?
15112.e: The law created a federal factory inspectorate. The inspectors visited factories and checked things like working hours.
15112.m: Factory inspectors made sure the Factory Act was followed.

15113.q: Which canton issued one of the first Swiss regulations against child labour in spinning mills in 1815?
15113.e: The Zurich regulation of 1815 banned children under 9 from factory work and also from night work. However, these rules could hardly be enforced.
15113.m: Zurich issued a regulation against child labour as early as 1815.

15114.q: What problem was often caused by child labour in factories?
a: The children could not go to school regularly.
The children had to do military service.
The children were not allowed to live with their parents.
The children had to pay taxes.
15114.e: Anyone standing in a factory for long hours could not go to school. In Prussia too, the breach of compulsory schooling was a main reason for the first protective laws.
15114.m: Child labour often stopped children from going to school.

15115.q: Which Swiss canton introduced the 12-hour day for adult factory workers too, with a Factory Act in 1864?
15115.e: In the textile canton of Glarus, the Landsgemeinde (open-air assembly) passed a Factory Act in 1864 against the government’s wishes, with a 12-hour day and a ban on night work. It is seen as a milestone in protecting workers, and the later federal Factory Act was based on the Glarus rules.
15115.m: Glarus introduced the 12-hour factory day by Landsgemeinde vote in 1864.

15116.q: Who were the “Verdingkinder” (contract children) in Switzerland?
a: Children who had to work for other families
Children who served in the army
15116.e: Poor or orphaned children were often sent to farming families, where they had to work hard. Many of them suffered great injustice, which Switzerland is now coming to terms with.
15116.m: Verdingkinder had to work for other families.

15117.q: With which sentence does “The Communist Manifesto” end?
15117.e: This call was meant to bring workers of all countries together. The sentence became a well-known slogan of the labour movement.
15117.m: The Communist Manifesto ends with “Workers of the world, unite!”

a: a group of employees working together for better working conditions
15118.e: In a trade union, workers join forces. Together they can fight more effectively for higher wages and shorter working hours.
15118.m: Trade unions stand up together for employees’ rights.

a: The factory is sold to a new owner.
15119.e: In a strike, many people stop working at the same time. In this way they put pressure on employers to meet their demands.
15119.m: In a strike, workers stop working together.

15120.q: In the 19th century, what was the name for workers’ many problems, such as poverty, illness and poor housing?
15120.e: With industrialisation, many working families lived in great hardship. How to solve this hardship was called the social question.
15120.m: The hardship of workers was called the social question.

15122.q: When it was founded in 1888, whose situation did the Social Democratic Party (SP) mainly want to improve?
15122.e: The SP was founded in 1888. It wanted to improve the situation of working people by democratic means, for example with shorter working hours and better wages.
15122.m: From the start, the SP stood up for workers.

15123.q: When did the general strike take place in Switzerland?
15123.e: From 12 to 14 November 1918, around 250,000 workers went on strike. It was the biggest strike in Swiss history.
15123.m: The general strike took place in November 1918.

15124.q: Who led the 1918 general strike as president of the Olten Action Committee?
15124.e: Robert Grimm was president of the Olten Action Committee. Because of the call to strike, he was sentenced to six months in prison in 1919.
15124.m: Robert Grimm led the general strike of 1918.

15125.q: Which demand of the 1918 general strike was put into practice in industry as early as 1919 and 1920?
15125.e: The 48-hour week was introduced in industry in 1919 and 1920. Women’s right to vote at federal level, on the other hand, only came in 1971.
15125.m: The 48-hour week was introduced soon after the general strike.

15126.q: Which social insurance, demanded during the 1918 general strike, only came into force in 1948?
15126.e: Old-age and survivors’ insurance (AHV) was one of the demands of the general strike. In the end it only came into force in 1948.
15126.m: The AHV was demanded in 1918 and introduced in 1948.

15127.q: What did the Federal Council use against the general strike in 1918?
15127.e: The Federal Council called up soldiers and gave the strikers an ultimatum. After three days the strike leaders called off the general strike. In Grenchen, three young workers were shot dead.
15127.m: The Federal Council ended the 1918 general strike with the army.

15128.q: Which day is known around the world as the labour movement’s “Labour Day”?
15128.e: On 1 May, trade unions in many countries demonstrate for employees’ rights. In some Swiss cantons it is a public holiday.

15129.q: What term did Marx and Engels use for the working class, which owns nothing but its ability to work?
15129.e: Proletarians do not own factories or machines. They live by selling their labour for wages.
15129.m: The proletariat is the working class that owns no property.

15130.q: Which Italian built the first usable battery, the voltaic pile, around 1800?
15130.e: Alessandro Volta presented his pile to the Royal Society in London in 1800. For the first time it produced a steady electric current.
15130.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.

15131.q: Which unit of electrical voltage is named after Alessandro Volta?
