19469.q: Which method finds all prime numbers up to a certain limit by crossing out multiples?
19469.e: With the sieve of Eratosthenes, you cross out all multiples of 2, 3, 5 and so on in turn. The prime numbers are what is left.
19469.m: The sieve of Eratosthenes goes back to an ancient Greek scholar.

19470.q: Which pair of numbers are twin primes?
19470.e: Twin primes are two prime numbers that are 2 apart. 15, 9 and 21 are not prime numbers.
19470.m: Twin primes are prime numbers that differ by exactly 2.

19471.q: Which of these numbers is divisible by 9?
19471.e: The digit sum of 7254 is 7 + 2 + 5 + 4, which is 18, and 18 is divisible by 9.
19471.m: A number is divisible by 9 if its digit sum is divisible by 9.

19472.q: Which of these numbers is divisible by 4?
19472.e: The last two digits, 16, form a number that is divisible by 4.
19472.m: A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4.

19473.q: What is the highest common factor (HCF) of 48 and 36?
19473.e: The factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Of these, 12 is the biggest that also divides 48.
19473.m: The HCF is the biggest number that divides both numbers with no remainder.

19474.q: What is the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 6 and 8?
19474.e: Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24. 24 is the first one that is also divisible by 6.
19474.m: The LCM is the smallest number that is a multiple of both numbers.

19475.q: How many factors does the number 36 have?
19475.e: The factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36, so 9 factors.
19475.m: Square numbers always have an odd number of factors.

19476.q: How can you tell that a number is divisible by 5?
19476.e: Every multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5, for example 35, 70 or 125.
19476.m: A number is divisible by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5.

19477.q: A bus leaves every 12 minutes, a tram every 18 minutes. At 8:00 both leave at the same time. When do they next leave at the same time?
19477.e: You need the LCM of 12 and 18, which is 36. So after 36 minutes, at 8:36.
19477.m: The lowest common multiple helps you find the next shared event.

19478.q: In a triangle, two angles measure 65° and 48°. How big is the third angle?
19478.e: The angles in a triangle add up to 180°. 180° − 65° − 48° makes 67°.
19478.m: The angles in a triangle always add up to 180 degrees.

19479.q: What do the angles in a quadrilateral add up to?
19479.e: A quadrilateral can be split into two triangles by a diagonal: 2 · 180° makes 360°.
19479.m: In every quadrilateral, the interior angles add up to 360 degrees.

19480.q: What do you call an angle that is bigger than 90° and smaller than 180°?
19480.e: Acute angles are smaller than 90°, and a straight angle measures exactly 180°. Obtuse angles lie in between.
19480.m: An obtuse angle lies between a right angle and a straight angle.

19481.q: A right-angled triangle has two shorter sides of 3 cm and 4 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
19481.e: According to Pythagoras' theorem, 3² + 4² makes 9 + 16, which is 25. The square root of 25 is 5.
19481.m: In a right-angled triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the hypotenuse.

19482.q: What is a quadrilateral with four sides of equal length whose angles are not right angles called?
19482.e: A rhombus (also called a diamond) has four sides of equal length. If all its angles are also right angles, it is a square.
19482.m: Every square is a special rhombus.

19483.q: What do the angles in a hexagon add up to?
19483.e: The angles in a polygon with n corners add up to (n − 2) · 180°. For n equal to 6: 4 · 180° makes 720°.
19483.m: With each extra corner, the angle sum grows by 180 degrees.

19484.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
19484.e: A square has two lines of symmetry through the midpoints of its sides and two along its diagonals.
19484.m: A rectangle that is not a square has only two lines of symmetry.

19485.q: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7 m wide. What is its area?
19485.e: The area of a rectangle is length times width: 12 m · 7 m makes 84 m².
19485.m: You work out the area of a rectangle as length times width.

19486.q: A triangle has a base of 10 cm and a height of 6 cm. What is its area?
19486.e: The area of a triangle is base times height divided by 2: 10 · 6 ÷ 2 makes 30 cm².
19486.m: A triangle is half the size of a rectangle with the same base and height.

19487.q: A trapezium has parallel sides of 8 cm and 4 cm and a height of 5 cm. What is its area?
19487.e: The area of a trapezium is (a + c) ÷ 2 · h, so (8 + 4) ÷ 2 · 5, which makes 6 · 5 and so 30 cm².
19487.m: For a trapezium, multiply the average of the parallel sides by the height.

19488.q: How many square centimetres are there in a square metre?
19488.e: A metre has 100 cm, so a square metre has 100 · 100, which makes 10,000 cm².
19488.m: For area units, the conversion factor between m² and dm² is 100.

19489.q: What is the area of a circle with a radius of 5 cm (rounded)?
19489.e: The area of a circle is π · r². 3.14159 · 25 makes about 78.5 cm².
19489.m: You work out the area of a circle as pi times the radius squared.

19490.q: How many square metres are there in a hectare?
19490.e: A hectare is a square of 100 m by 100 m, so 10,000 m².
19490.m: A hectare is a bit bigger than a football pitch.

19491.q: A square has an area of 64 cm². What is its perimeter?
19491.e: The side length is the square root of 64, so 8 cm. The perimeter is 4 · 8 cm, which makes 32 cm.
19491.m: You get the side length of a square from its area with the square root.

19492.q: A cuboid is 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. What is its volume?
19492.e: The volume of a cuboid is length times width times height: 5 · 4 · 3 makes 60 cm³.
19492.m: You work out the volume of a cuboid as length times width times height.

19493.q: What is the volume of a cube with edges 3 cm long?
19493.e: For a cube, you work out the edge to the power of 3: 3 · 3 · 3 makes 27 cm³.
19493.m: The volume of a cube is the edge length to the power of three.

19494.q: How many litres fit into a cubic metre?
19494.e: A litre is the same as a cubic decimetre, and a cubic metre has 10 · 10 · 10, which makes 1,000 dm³.
19494.m: A litre is the same as a cubic decimetre.

19495.q: How many millilitres are equal to one cubic centimetre?
19495.e: A litre has 1,000 ml and 1,000 cm³. That is why 1 cm³ is exactly 1 ml.
19495.m: A cubic centimetre holds exactly one millilitre.

19496.q: An aquarium is 50 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high. How many litres of water fit into it?
19496.e: 50 · 30 · 40 makes 60,000 cm³. That is 60,000 ml or 60 litres.
19496.m: To get litres, divide cubic centimetres by 1,000.

19497.q: What is the volume of a cylinder with a radius of 2 cm and a height of 10 cm (rounded)?
19497.e: The volume is the base area times the height: π · 2² · 10 makes 40π, about 125.7 cm³.
19497.m: The volume of a cylinder is the area of the circle times the height.

19498.q: All the edges of a cube are doubled. How does its volume change?
19498.e: The volume depends on three edges: 2 · 2 · 2 gives a factor of 8.
19498.m: If you double all the lengths of a solid, its volume becomes eight times as big.

19499.q: In which quadrant is the point (-3, 5)?
19499.e: The x value is negative and the y value is positive. That is top left, so the 2nd quadrant.
19499.m: The quadrants are numbered anticlockwise starting at the top right.

19500.q: What is the horizontal axis in a coordinate system called?
19500.e: The horizontal axis is the x-axis (abscissa), the vertical one is the y-axis (ordinate).
19500.m: For a point, you always give the x value first and then the y value.

19501.q: What are the coordinates of the origin of a coordinate system?
19501.e: The origin is where the two axes cross. There, x and y are both 0.
19501.m: The x-axis and the y-axis cross at the origin.

19502.q: Which point is exactly halfway between A(2, 3) and B(8, 7)?
19502.e: You take the average each time: (2 + 8) ÷ 2 makes 5 and (3 + 7) ÷ 2 makes 5.
19502.m: You find the midpoint of a line segment using the averages of the coordinates.

19503.q: The point P(4, -2) is reflected in the x-axis. Where is the image point?
19503.e: When reflecting in the x-axis, the x value stays the same and the y value changes its sign.
19503.m: When reflecting in the x-axis, only the y value changes its sign.

19504.q: How far apart are the points A(1, 2) and B(7, 10) (in units)?
19504.e: The differences are 6 and 8. With Pythagoras: the square root of 36 + 64, so of 100, makes 10.
19504.m: Distances in a coordinate system are worked out with Pythagoras' theorem.

19505.q: Which point lies on the line y = 2x + 1?
19505.e: If you put in x equal to 3, 2 · 3 + 1 gives the value 7. The other points do not satisfy the equation.
19505.m: A point lies on a line if its coordinates satisfy the equation.

19506.q: Which type of chart is best for showing parts of a whole?
19506.e: In a pie chart, the whole circle stands for 100 %, and the sectors show the parts.
19506.m: A pie chart shows how a whole is divided into parts.

19507.q: Which type of chart best shows how the temperature changes over a day?
19507.e: A line graph joins up measurements over time and makes rises and falls visible.
19507.m: Changes over time are shown well with a line graph.

19508.q: In a pie chart, 25 % stands for the cyclists. How big is the angle of this sector?
19508.e: The whole circle is 360°. 25 % of it is 360° ÷ 4, which makes 90°.
19508.m: In a pie chart, 100 % is exactly 360 degrees.

19509.q: Of 30 children, 12 like pizza best. How big is the pizza sector in a pie chart?
19509.m: You work out the sector angle as the fraction times 360 degrees.

19510.q: A bar chart shows break-time rolls sold from Monday to Friday: 4, 7, 5, 8, 6. What is the average per day?
19510.e: The total is 4 + 7 + 5 + 8 + 6, which is 30. Divided by 5 days, that makes 6.
19510.m: You get the average by adding up all the values and dividing by how many there are.

19511.q: What is the median of the values 3, 9, 4, 7 and 5?
19511.e: In order of size: 3, 4, 5, 7, 9. The middle value is 5.
19511.m: The median is the middle value of a list sorted by size.

19512.q: What is a diagram called that uses circles to show what sets have in common and how they differ?
19512.e: In a Venn diagram, each circle stands for a set. The overlap shows what belongs to both sets.
19512.m: A Venn diagram shows intersections of sets.

19513.q: Solve the equation 3x + 5 = 23. What is x?
19513.e: First subtract 5: 3x makes 18. Then divide by 3: x is 6.
19513.m: An equation stays true if you do the same thing to both sides.

19514.q: Solve the equation 4x − 7 = 3x − 9. What is x?
19514.e: Subtract 3x from both sides: x − 7 makes -9. Then add 7: x is -2.
19514.m: You bring all the x terms to one side and all the numbers to the other.

19515.q: For which value of x is x ÷ 7 = 8?
19515.e: You multiply both sides by 7: x is 8 · 7, which is 56.

19516.q: Solve the equation 2(x + 3) = 16. What is x?
19516.e: Divide both sides by 2: x + 3 makes 8. Then subtract 3: x is 5.
19516.m: With brackets, you divide first or multiply out the bracket.

19517.q: Mia is 4 years older than her brother. Together they are 30 years old. How old is her brother?
19517.e: With x for the brother, x + (x + 4) makes 30, so 2x equals 26 and x equals 13.
19517.m: You solve word problems by calling the unknown x and setting up an equation.

19518.e: You collect like terms: 5x − 3x makes 2x, and then add + 2.
19518.m: You may only collect like terms, such as x and x.

19519.q: What are the solutions of the equation x² = 49?
19519.m: A quadratic equation can have two solutions.

19520.q: On a balance, there are 3 balls of equal weight on the left, and 2 such balls and a 12 kg weight on the right. The balance is level. How heavy is one ball?
19520.e: 3x equals 2x + 12. If you take 2 balls off each side, x equals 12 kg is left.
19520.m: A balance that is level behaves like an equation.

19521.q: I think of a number, multiply it by 3 and add 4. The result is 25. Which number did I think of?
19521.m: You often solve number puzzles by working backwards.

19522.q: What is the next number in the sequence 2, 6, 18, 54, ...?
19522.e: Each number is three times the one before: 54 · 3 makes 162.
19522.m: With number sequences, look for the rule that gets you from one number to the next.

19523.q: What is the next number in the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...?
19523.e: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 8 + 13 makes 21. This is the Fibonacci sequence.
19523.m: In the Fibonacci sequence, each number is the sum of the two before it.

19524.q: What is the next number in the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...?
19524.e: These are the square numbers 1², 2², 3², 4², 5². Next comes 6², which is 36.
19524.m: Square numbers come from multiplying a number by itself.

19525.q: Two numbers add up to 20, and their difference is 6. What is the bigger number?
19525.e: The bigger number is (20 + 6) ÷ 2, which is 13. The smaller one is 7, and 13 − 7 makes 6.
19525.m: With a sum and a difference, the bigger number is half of the two added together.

19526.q: A two-digit number has a digit sum of 9. The tens digit is twice the ones digit. Which number is it?
19526.e: With ones digit e, 2e + e makes 9, so e equals 3. The tens digit is 6, so the number is 63.
19526.m: In digit puzzles, it helps to look at the tens digit and the ones digit separately.

19527.q: On a farm there are hens and rabbits, with 10 heads and 28 legs altogether. How many rabbits are there?
19527.e: If all 10 animals had 2 legs, there would be 20 legs. The 8 extra legs are shared out 2 each among 4 rabbits.
19527.m: In heads-and-legs puzzles, first work it out as if all the animals were the same.

19528.q: What is the probability of rolling a 6 with a normal dice?
19528.e: A dice has 6 equally likely sides, and only one of them shows the 6.
19528.m: Probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the number of possible outcomes.

19529.q: What is the probability of rolling an even number with a dice?
19529.e: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, so 3 out of 6 possibilities. 3/6 simplifies to 1/2.
19529.m: Count the favourable outcomes carefully before you write the fraction.

19530.q: You roll two dice. What is the probability that the total is 7?
19530.e: Of 36 possible pairs, 6 give a total of 7: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1. 6/36 makes 1/6.
19530.m: With two dice there are 36 equally likely outcomes.

19531.q: You toss a coin three times. What is the probability of getting heads three times?
19531.m: For independent events, you multiply the probabilities.

19532.q: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. What is the probability of drawing a red ball without looking?
19532.e: There are 10 balls, 5 of them red. 5/10 makes 1/2.
19532.m: The more balls of one colour there are in the bag, the more likely you are to draw that colour.

19533.q: What is the probability of an impossible event?
19533.e: Probabilities lie between 0 and 1. An impossible event has 0, a certain event has 1.
19533.m: A certain event has a probability of 1.

19534.q: What is the probability of NOT rolling a 6 with a dice?
19534.e: The opposite of “a 6” has a probability of 1 − 1/6, which is 5/6.
19534.m: The probability of the opposite event is 1 minus the probability of the event.

19535.q: In how many different ways can 3 children line up in a row?
19535.e: There are 3 possibilities for the first place, 2 for the second and 1 for the last: 3 · 2 · 1 makes 6.
19535.m: The number of orders of n things is n factorial.

19544.q: What is the solution of the equation 3x + 7 = 22?
19544.e: You subtract 7 and get 3x equals 15. Dividing by 3 gives x equals 5.
19544.m: With equations, always do the same step on both sides.

19548.q: What is the solution of the equation 2x/3 − 4 = 6?
19548.e: You add 4 and get 2x/3 equals 10. Multiplying by 3/2 gives x equals 15.
19548.m: You remove a fraction in front of the variable by multiplying by its reciprocal.

19593.q: How many different four-digit PIN codes using the digits 0 to 9 are there?
19593.e: Each of the 4 places can be one of 10 digits, and repeats are allowed. That makes 10⁴, which is 10,000.
19593.m: When choosing with repetition and order, you work out n to the power of k.

19598.q: A restaurant offers 3 starters, 4 main courses and 2 desserts. How many different menus with one course from each group are there?
19598.e: By the product rule, you multiply the possibilities: 3 · 4 · 2 makes 24.
19598.m: Independent choices are multiplied by the product rule.

20218.q: What does the internet connect all over the world?
20218.e: The internet is a huge network. In it, computers, phones and other devices all over the world are connected to each other.
20218.m: The internet connects computers all over the world.

20219.q: What does the abbreviation “www” in internet addresses stand for?
20219.e: “www” stands for “World Wide Web”, a network that spans the whole world.
20219.m: The abbreviation www means World Wide Web.

20220.q: Near which Swiss city was the World Wide Web invented?
20220.e: Tim Berners-Lee presented his idea for the World Wide Web in 1989 at the CERN research centre near Geneva.
20220.m: The World Wide Web was invented at CERN near Geneva.

20221.e: If you are online, you are connected to the internet. If you are not connected, you are offline.
20221.m: Online means being connected to the internet.

20222.q: What is the wireless network that lets devices at home get onto the internet called?
20222.e: Wi-Fi is a network without cables. It connects phones, tablets and computers to the internet.
20222.m: With Wi-Fi you can get onto the internet without a cable.

20223.q: Which device at home often shares the internet with all the other devices?
20223.e: The router is a small box. It connects the home to the internet and often also provides the Wi-Fi.
20223.m: The router brings the internet into the home.

20224.q: What can you not do directly on the internet?
20224.e: On the internet you can read, watch, listen and write. You cannot send smells over it.
20224.m: On the internet you can read, watch, listen and write.

20225.q: Is everything on the internet true?
a: Yes, if there is a picture
20225.e: Anyone can write something on the internet. That is why there are also mistakes and lies there.
20225.m: Not everything on the internet is true.

20226.q: What is the best thing to do if you are not sure whether something on the internet is true?
20226.e: Adults can help you check something. You can also look it up in a book or on a second website.
20226.m: If I am not sure, I ask an adult.

20227.q: What is a page on the internet that you can look at called?
20227.e: A web page is a page on the World Wide Web. Several web pages together make up a website.
20227.m: A page on the internet is called a web page.

20228.q: Which program do you use to look at web pages?
20228.e: A browser is a program for showing web pages. You type the address at the top.
20228.m: You look at web pages with a browser.

20229.q: Which ending do many Swiss internet addresses have?
20229.e: The ending .ch stands for Switzerland. It comes from the Latin name “Confoederatio Helvetica”.

20230.q: What happens when you click on a link?
20230.e: A link is a connection to another page. With one click you jump there.
20230.m: A link takes me to another page.

20231.q: Where do you type the address of a web page?
20231.e: The address bar is right at the top of the browser. That is where you write an address, for example one ending in .ch.
20231.m: You type a web page's address in the address bar at the top.

20232.q: What does a small padlock next to the address in the browser often show?
20232.e: The padlock shows that the data is sent encrypted. But it does not mean that the site is safe or honest.
20232.m: A padlock in the browser shows an encrypted connection.

20233.q: What should you do if a website frightens you?
20233.e: Some websites show things that are not good for children. Close the page and tell someone you trust.
20233.m: If something frightens me, I close the page and tell someone.

20234.q: What is the first page you see on a website called?
20234.e: The home page is the first page of a website. From there you can get to the other pages.
20234.m: The first page of a website is called the home page.

20235.q: What do you need a search engine for?
20235.e: A search engine searches the internet. It shows a list of matching web pages.
20235.m: With a search engine I find web pages.

20236.q: What do you type into a search engine?
20236.e: You type in one or more words that fit the topic. The search engine then looks for pages with these words.
20236.m: I type suitable search words into a search engine.

20237.q: Are there search engines made especially for children?
20237.e: There are search engines for children. They mainly show pages that are suitable for children.
20237.m: There are special search engines for children.

20238.q: Are the first results of a search always the best?
a: Yes, always on children's search engines
20238.e: At the very top there are often adverts that someone has paid for. That is why it is worth looking carefully.
20238.m: The first result is not always the best.

20239.q: What is a good search for animals in the forest?
20239.e: Good search words are short and fit the topic exactly. You leave out unnecessary words.
20239.m: Short, fitting search words help when searching.

20240.q: What do you call the results a search engine shows?
20240.e: After a search, the search engine shows lots of results. These results are also called hits.
20240.m: The results of a search are called hits.

20241.q: What can help if you cannot find anything suitable?
20241.e: Sometimes the words do not fit well. With different or more exact words, you often find more.
20241.m: If I find nothing, I try other search words.

20242.q: What does a search engine's image search show?
20242.e: In an image search, the search engine shows pictures that match the search word. You are not allowed to reuse every picture just like that.
20242.m: Image search shows pictures for my search word.

20243.e: App is short for “application”. It is a program, for example for games, photos or the weather.
20243.m: An app is a program for a phone or tablet.

20244.q: Where do you usually download apps from?
20244.e: You get apps from an app store. It is a shop for apps on a phone or tablet.
20244.m: You download apps from an app store.

20245.q: Who do you ask before you download a new app?
20245.e: Some apps cost money or collect data. That is why children ask their parents first.
20245.m: Before getting a new app, I ask my parents.

20246.q: What does the age rating on an app show?
a: From what age it is suitable
How long it takes to load
20246.e: The age rating says which age an app is suitable for. That way you can see whether it is right for children.
20246.m: The age rating shows from what age an app is suitable.

20247.q: Can free apps cost money too?
a: Yes, through purchases in the app
20247.e: Many free apps offer extras to buy. These are called in-app purchases.
20247.m: Even a free app can cost money.

20248.q: What is the small picture you tap to open an app called?
20248.e: Every app has a small picture on the screen. It is called an icon.
20248.m: I open an app by tapping its icon.

20249.q: Why should you update apps now and then?
a: So that they get more colourful
So that they show more adverts
So that the phone charges faster
20249.e: An update fixes mistakes. That way the app and the device stay better protected.

20250.q: What do you do with an app you no longer need?
20250.e: You do not need unnecessary apps. If you delete them, the device has more space and collects less data.
20250.m: I can delete apps I do not need.

20251.q: What is a letter you send over the internet called?
20251.e: An email is an electronic letter. It usually arrives within a few seconds.
20251.m: An email is a letter sent over the internet.

20252.q: Which symbol is in every email address?
20252.e: The @ symbol separates the name from the provider. It is read as “at”.

20253.q: What are the little pictures, like a smiling face, in messages called?
20253.e: Emojis are small pictures. They show feelings or things, for example a heart or a sun.
20253.m: Emojis are little pictures in messages.

20254.q: What do you do with a message from a stranger?
20254.e: You can never be sure who is behind a message from a stranger. That is why you show it to your parents.
20254.m: I show messages from strangers to my parents.

20255.q: Can you reliably take back a message completely once it is sent?
a: Yes, if it has a picture
20255.e: Whoever received the message can save it or send it on. That is why you think before sending.
20255.m: I think before I send a message.

a: A chat with lots of people
20256.e: In a group chat, several people write together. Everyone in the group can read everything.
20256.m: In a group chat, everyone can read along.

20257.q: How does a message written only in capital letters come across?
20257.e: Whole words in capital letters often come across like shouting in a chat. That is why you write normally.
20257.m: All capitals come across like shouting in a chat.

20258.q: What should you do with a chain message that threatens you?
a: Print it out and hang it up
20258.e: Chain messages often threaten bad luck if you do not send them on. That is not true; you can delete them.
20258.m: I do not send chain messages on.

20259.e: A password is like a key. Only someone who knows it can get into the account.
20259.m: A password is like a key.

20260.q: Who may you tell your password to?
20260.e: A password stays secret. Only your parents may know it, so that they can help.
20260.m: Only my parents and I know my password.

20261.q: Why is your first name not a good password?
20261.e: Lots of people know your name. So a password like that is easy to guess.
20261.m: My name is not a good password.

20262.q: What do you do if someone knows your password?
a: Write it down and hang it up
20262.e: If another person knows the password, the account is no longer protected. It is best to change it together with your parents.
20262.m: If someone knows my password, I change it.

20263.q: Should you use a different password for every account?
20263.e: Otherwise, if one password is stolen, all your accounts are in danger. With different passwords, the damage stays small.
20263.m: I use a separate password for every account.

20264.q: Where is the worst place to keep a note with a password?
20264.e: Anyone can read a note on the screen. Then the password is no longer secret.
20264.m: I do not stick my password to the screen.

20265.q: How do you usually see a password while typing it?
a: Not at all, it just beeps
20265.e: While you type, the screen usually only shows dots or asterisks. That way nobody can read the password over your shoulder.
20265.m: My password is usually hidden while I type it.

20266.q: Which of these is part of your personal data?
20266.e: Personal data says something about you, for example what your name is or where you live.
20266.m: My address is part of my personal data.

20267.q: May you tell a stranger on the internet your address?
20267.e: Anyone who knows your address knows where you live. That is why it stays secret on the internet.
20267.m: I do not give away my address on the internet.

20268.q: What is best to use as a name in a game?
20268.e: A made-up name does not give away who you are. This protects you on the internet.
20268.m: On the internet I use a made-up name.

20269.q: Why should you not post a photo of yourself in front of your school online?
a: People can see where I am
20269.e: You can recognise the place in the photo. Strangers could find out where you often are.
20269.m: In photos online, I do not show where I am.

20270.q: Who do you ask before sending a photo of a friend?
a: The teacher of the class next door
20270.e: Everyone may decide for themselves where photos of them end up. That is why you always ask first.
20270.m: Before sharing a photo, I ask the person in it.

20271.q: Is a photo on the internet definitely gone if you delete it?
20271.e: Others may already have saved the photo or sent it on. So it might still be somewhere.
20271.m: What is on the internet often stays there for a long time.

20272.q: Which detail is fine to show in a game?
20272.e: A favourite colour does not give away who you are or where you live. So it is harmless.
20272.m: I can show harmless things like my favourite colour.

20273.q: Should you show your date of birth everywhere on the internet?
20273.e: Your date of birth is personal data. Together with your name, it can help people find you.
20273.m: I do not show my date of birth to everyone on the internet.

20274.q: What do you do if something on the internet seems strange to you?
20274.e: Adults can help and solve the problem. Nobody has to deal with it alone.
20274.m: If something seems strange, I tell an adult.

20275.q: Which number can children and young people in Switzerland call when they have worries?
20275.e: On 147, Pro Juventute's advice service helps. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 144 the emergency number for an ambulance.
20275.m: In Switzerland, I can call 147 when I have worries.

20276.q: What do you do if a window says “You have won, click here”?
20276.e: Windows like this are often tricks. They want to steal data or put harmful programs on the device.
20276.m: When I see “You have won”, I do not click.

20277.e: A computer virus is a program that causes damage. It can delete data or disrupt the device.
20277.m: A computer virus is a harmful program.

20278.q: Where is the best place for young children to surf the internet?
20278.e: If parents are nearby, they can help quickly. That is why the living room is often a good place.
20278.m: I surf where my parents are nearby.

20279.q: What do you do if someone threatens you on the internet?
a: Delete the chat and keep quiet
20279.e: Parents or teachers can help. You can keep the message as evidence.
20279.m: I show threats on the internet to my parents.

20280.q: Is it your fault if someone sends you something nasty on the internet?
a: Yes, if I know the person
20280.e: The fault lies with the person who sends something nasty. If you tell someone, you are doing everything right.
20280.m: It is not my fault if someone sends me something nasty.

20281.q: What is best to do with attachments in emails from strangers?
20281.e: Attachments from strangers can contain harmful programs. That is why you do not open them.
20281.m: I do not open attachments from strangers.

20282.q: Who helps you with a problem on the internet if your parents are not there?
20282.e: Teachers and other adults you trust are happy to help. Strangers on the internet are not the right people for this.
20282.m: A person I trust helps me with problems.

20283.q: Do you always know who is behind a profile on the internet?
20283.e: On the internet, people can use a false name and a false photo. A child in a chat might really be an adult.
20283.m: On the internet I never know for sure who is writing.

20284.q: What do you do if an online friend wants to meet you?
20284.e: You never meet anyone from the internet alone. Your parents decide and come with you.
20284.m: I only meet online friends together with my parents.

20285.q: What if someone in a chat says “This is our secret”?
20285.e: Good friends do not ask you to keep secrets from your parents. Sentences like this are a warning sign.
20285.m: I tell my parents about bad secrets.

20286.q: Who is usually a real friend?
20286.e: You know real friends from everyday life, for example from school. With strangers online, you cannot be sure.
20286.m: I know my real friends in real life too.

20287.q: What do you do if someone online asks you for photos of yourself?
a: Send a photo of my house
20287.e: Photos of you belong to you. Strangers who want photos often do not mean well.
20287.m: I do not send photos of myself to strangers.

20288.q: Are you allowed to block someone in a chat?
a: Yes, if they are bothering you
20288.e: Anyone who is mean or bothers you can be blocked. Then that person can no longer write to you.
20288.m: I can block anyone who bothers me.

20289.q: What do you do if an online friend promises you presents?
20289.e: Strangers sometimes promise presents to win your trust. That is why you tell your parents.
20289.m: I am careful about presents from strangers on the internet.

20290.q: Can you have friends online too?
a: Yes, and you tell them everything
20290.e: Online you can play nicely with others. But you do not give away personal details.
20290.m: I can have friends online too, but I stay careful.

a: Time spent in front of a phone or TV
20291.e: Screen time is the time you spend in front of a screen. That includes phones, tablets, computers and TVs.
20291.m: Screen time is the time spent in front of screens.

20292.q: What is good after you have spent a long time at a screen?
20292.e: Exercise is good for your body. Playing outside is a good balance.
20292.m: After screen time, I move about.

20293.q: When is not a good time for phones and tablets?
20293.e: Light and excitement from the screen can make it harder to fall asleep. That is why you put devices away beforehand.
20293.m: I put the screen away before going to sleep.

20294.q: Who helps set screen time for children?
20294.e: Parents and children can make rules together. Then it is clear how long and when you play.
20294.m: I make rules about screen time with my parents.

20295.q: What can help you stop on time?
20295.e: A timer reminds you when the time is up. That makes it easier to stop.

20296.q: What can happen if you look at a screen for a very long time?
20296.e: Looking at a screen for a long time strains the eyes. Breaks help them recover.
20296.m: Breaks are good for my eyes.

20297.q: What is a good rule at mealtimes at the family table?
20297.e: At mealtimes, people talk to each other. Without a phone, you have more time for each other.
20297.m: The phone stays away at mealtimes.

20298.q: What is a good activity without a screen?
20298.e: You play a board game together at the table. It does not need a screen.
20298.m: Without a screen I can play board games.

20299.q: Why is a break good when playing on a screen?
20299.e: During a break you can stand up, have a drink and stretch. That way your body and mind recover.
20299.m: I take breaks when playing on a screen.

20300.e: Advertising shows things looking especially nice. It is meant to make you want to buy something.
20300.m: Advertising wants me to buy something.

20301.q: How can you often recognise advertising on the internet?
20301.e: Advertising often has to be labelled. You then read “Ad”, “Advert” or “Sponsored”.

20302.q: Does a toy always look as great in real life as in the advert?
20302.e: Adverts show things in the best light. In real life they are often smaller or less exciting.
20302.m: Adverts make things look better than they are.

20303.q: What is an advertising film before a video?
20303.e: Before many videos, a short advert clip plays first. It wants to sell something.
20303.m: A short advertising film is called an advert clip.

20304.q: What do you do if a game pushes you to buy something?
20304.e: Games often tempt you with extras that cost money. Children do not buy anything without their parents.
20304.m: I do not buy anything on the internet without my parents.

20305.q: What do people in internet videos sometimes show because they are paid to?
a: Toys and other things to buy
20305.e: Some people show things in their videos that a company pays for. That is advertising too.
20305.m: There is hidden advertising in videos too.

20306.q: Why are there so many free games with adverts?
a: The adverts make the game faster
20306.e: People who make a game want to earn money. Companies often pay for adverts to be shown in the game.
20306.m: Free games often earn money through adverts.

20307.q: How can you close an unwanted advert in a window?
20307.e: The small X closes a window. Clicking on the picture usually takes you to the advertiser's page. Sometimes even the X is a trick, so if in doubt ask an adult.
20307.m: I close a window with the small X.

20308.q: How should people treat each other on the internet?
a: In a friendly and polite way
20308.e: On the internet too, there are real people behind the messages. That is why you write kindly.
20308.m: I am friendly on the internet.

20309.q: What are the rules for good behaviour on the internet called?
20309.e: The word netiquette comes from “net” and “etiquette”, which means good manners.
20309.m: Netiquette is the set of rules for good behaviour online.

20310.e: In cyberbullying, someone is picked on, laughed at or threatened on the internet again and again. That hurts a lot.
20310.m: Cyberbullying means picking on someone on the internet.

20311.q: What do you do if someone in your class is being picked on online?
20311.e: Helping is brave. A teacher or parents can stop the bullying.
20311.m: If someone is being picked on, I get help.

20312.q: Which question helps before sending a message?
a: Would I say it to their face?
Does it have lots of colours?
Is it funny just for me?
20312.e: If you would not say it to someone's face, do not write it either. That way you stay respectful.
20312.m: I only write what I would also say to someone's face.

20313.q: What does a thumbs-up in a chat often mean?
20313.e: A thumbs-up usually means “good” or “agreed”. You can show feelings with emojis.
20313.m: A thumbs-up often means I like something.

20314.q: Is it all right to spread rumours about others on the internet?
20314.e: Rumours can hurt people very badly. What is online spreads quickly.
20314.m: I do not spread rumours about others.

20315.q: What do you say if you have hurt someone in a chat?
20315.e: An apology shows that you are sorry. That is important online too.
20315.m: If I have hurt someone, I apologise.

20316.q: How do you write a comment on a friend's picture?
20316.e: A kind comment makes the other person happy. You can give criticism in a friendly way.
20316.m: I write comments kindly and honestly.

20317.q: What is the Swiss law that governs how personal data is handled called?
20317.e: The Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP) governs how personal data may be processed. The revised version has applied since 1 September 2023.
20317.m: The Data Protection Act protects people's data in Switzerland.

20318.q: Since when has Switzerland's revised Data Protection Act applied?
20318.e: The fully revised Data Protection Act came into force on 1 September 2023. It adapts data protection to the digital world.
20318.m: The new Data Protection Act has applied in Switzerland since 2023.

20319.q: A torch app wants access to your contacts, photos and location. What is the problem with this?
a: It collects more data than it needs
It makes the light too bright
It only works during the day
20319.e: Under the Data Protection Act, only data needed for the purpose may be processed. A torch needs neither contacts nor location. In Switzerland, the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC) watches over such rules.
20319.m: An app should only get the data it really needs.

20320.e: Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable person, for example a name, address, photo or phone number.
20320.m: Everything that belongs to a particular person is personal data.

20321.q: Which data counts as especially sensitive under the Data Protection Act?
20321.e: Especially sensitive data includes, for example, data about health, religion, political views or ethnic origin. Stricter rules apply to it.

20322.q: What is the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation usually abbreviated to?
20322.e: The GDPR has applied in all EU countries since 25 May 2018. Swiss companies must also follow it when they process data about people in the EU.
20322.m: The GDPR is the data protection law of the European Union.

20323.q: What are cookies on the internet?
a: Small text files in the browser
20323.e: Cookies are small files that a website stores in the browser. With them it can remember settings, but also track how you surf.
20323.m: Cookies store information about my visit to a website.

20324.q: What does it mean when an app asks for “permission” to use the microphone?
a: It wants to access the microphone
It wants to repair the microphone
It wants to turn the volume down
It wants to lock the phone
20324.e: With permissions, you allow an app to access features such as the camera, location or microphone. You should only allow what the app really needs.
20324.m: I only give an app the permissions it really needs.

a: Repeatedly humiliating someone through digital media
A one-off argument in the playground
20325.e: In cyberbullying, someone is deliberately and repeatedly insulted, threatened or humiliated by phone or on the internet.
20325.m: Cyberbullying is bullying using digital media.

20326.q: Why is cyberbullying often especially hard to bear?
a: It can go on round the clock
It only lasts a few minutes
20326.e: On the internet, the bullying does not stop after school. Also, posts can quickly be seen and spread by lots of people.
20326.m: Cyberbullying can follow the people affected everywhere.

20327.q: What should people affected by cyberbullying do to keep evidence?
20327.e: Screenshots showing the date and sender can later be used to prove attacks to the school or the police.
20327.m: If I am cyberbullied, I keep evidence with screenshots.

20328.q: Which Pro Juventute phone number can children and young people in Switzerland call when they have worries?
20328.e: The number 147 is Pro Juventute's advice service for children and young people. It is free and confidential and can also be reached by chat.
20328.m: In Switzerland, the number 147 helps when you have worries.

20329.q: What are people called who see cyberbullying but do not step in?
20329.e: Bystanders play an important role. If they get help or support the person affected, bullying can often be stopped.
20329.m: Anyone who sees cyberbullying should get help instead of just watching.

20330.q: Which feature in most apps stops a person from writing to you any more?
20330.e: If you block a person, they usually cannot send you messages any more. You can also report harassing content to the platform.
20330.m: I can block people who harass me.

20331.q: Can cyberbullying be a criminal offence in Switzerland, even though (as of 2026) there is no specific offence for it yet?
a: Yes, for example as insult or threat
No, no laws apply on the internet
Only if it lasts longer than a year
20331.e: The Criminal Code includes offences such as insult, defamation, threats and coercion, which also apply online. In 2026, a specific offence against bullying was still only a draft under consultation.
20331.m: The law applies on the internet too.

20332.e: Fake news is false information spread on purpose that looks like real news. It is meant to deceive or influence people, or to get clicks.
20332.m: Fake news is deliberately false news.

20333.e: In a fact check, experts use reliable sources to check whether a statement is true. Many media outlets have their own teams for this.
20333.m: A fact check tests whether a claim is true.

a: A sensational headline meant to get you to click
20334.e: Clickbait is bait to make you click. Exaggerated headlines lure readers in, but the content often does not deliver what was promised.
20334.m: Sensational headlines are meant to tempt me to click.

20335.q: What makes satire different from fake news?
a: Satire exaggerates in an obvious way to entertain or criticise
20335.e: Satire exaggerates on purpose and wants to make you think or laugh. It becomes a problem when it is shared out of context and taken to be real.
20335.m: Satire uses exaggeration to criticise, not to deceive.

20336.q: What should you check before sharing a surprising news story?
a: Whether other reliable sources report the same
How many emojis the story has
Whether the picture is in colour
20336.e: If several independent and reliable media report the same thing, a story is more likely to be true. If in doubt, it is better not to share it.
20336.m: Before sharing, I check whether reliable sources report the same.

20337.q: What is a computer program that automatically spreads posts on social networks called?
20337.e: Social bots are programs that behave like real users. They can spread false reports quickly and on a huge scale.
20337.m: Behind some accounts there is no person, but a program.

20338.q: How can you find out whether a photo has appeared before in a different context?
20338.e: In a reverse image search, you upload a picture to a search engine. This shows you where and when it has already been published.
20338.m: With a reverse image search I can find out where a photo comes from.

20339.q: What minimum age do most big social networks require in their terms of use?
20339.e: According to their rules, platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat require a minimum age of 13. This has to do with data protection for children.
20339.m: Most social networks are only allowed from 13.

20340.q: Who founded the social network Facebook in 2004?
20340.e: Mark Zuckerberg founded Facebook in 2004 as a student at Harvard University, together with fellow students.
20340.m: Facebook was founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004.

20341.q: Which company owns Instagram and WhatsApp?
20341.e: Facebook bought Instagram in 2012 and WhatsApp in 2014. Since 2021 the company has been called Meta.
20341.m: Instagram and WhatsApp belong to the company Meta.

20342.q: What has the short message service Twitter been called since 2023?
20342.e: After it was taken over by Elon Musk, Twitter was renamed X in 2023.
20342.m: Since 2023, Twitter has been called X.

20343.q: What is a hashtag like #Switzerland on social networks for?
a: Making posts on a topic easy to find
20343.e: The hash sign marks keywords. If you tap on the hashtag, you see all public posts on that word.
20343.m: Hashtags collect posts on a topic.

20344.q: How long are Instagram stories normally visible?
20344.e: Stories disappear automatically for others after 24 hours. Even so, they can be saved permanently with screenshots.
20344.m: Even stories that disappear can be saved.

20345.q: Which country does ByteDance, the company that owns TikTok, come from?
20345.e: ByteDance was founded in Beijing in 2012. TikTok is the international sister app of the Chinese app Douyin.
20345.m: TikTok was developed by the Chinese company ByteDance.

20346.q: What does the “private account” setting on social networks usually do?
a: Only approved followers see the posts
You can no longer post photos
20346.e: With a private account, you have to approve follower requests. Strangers then cannot see your posts without permission.
20346.m: With a private account, I decide who sees my posts.

a: A person who influences lots of people through social media
20347.e: Influencers have lots of followers and influence opinions and buying decisions with their posts. Many earn money from it.
20347.m: Influencers influence many people with their posts.

20348.q: How do many influencers earn their money?
a: From a salary paid by the state
20348.e: Companies pay influencers to show or recommend products. They also earn money from adverts shown before videos.
20348.m: Many influencers are paid for advertising.

a: Advertising that cannot be recognised as advertising
20349.e: In hidden advertising, the fact that a recommendation was paid for is kept quiet. This is unfair, because advertising must be recognisable.
20349.m: Paid advertising must be recognisable as advertising.

20350.q: How should influencers label paid posts?
a: With a red frame around the picture
Not at all, it is optional
20350.e: Commercial communication must be clearly recognisable as such. In Switzerland, the Swiss Commission for Fairness requires this in its principles.

a: How many people see their posts
20351.e: Reach shows how many people a post or an account reaches. It is an important figure for advertisers.
20351.m: Reach shows how many people are reached.

a: A product is deliberately shown in return for payment
A product is rearranged in a shop
A product is given away free
20352.e: In product placement, a branded product is shown visibly in a video or film because the maker pays for it.
20352.m: When a product is shown for money, it is advertising.

20353.q: Why do influencers often show a particularly beautiful picture of their lives?
a: Because posts are chosen and edited
Because their lives are always perfect
Because cameras only film nice things
20353.e: On social media, many people only show chosen moments, often edited with filters. This can give a false picture of everyday life.
20353.m: Social media often only shows the nicest moments of life.

a: A clear sequence of instructions for solving a task
20354.e: An algorithm describes step by step how a problem is solved. A recipe works in a similar way.
20354.m: An algorithm is a set of step-by-step instructions.

20355.q: What does a video app's algorithm mainly use to choose what is shown to you?
20355.e: Recommendation algorithms analyse what you watch, like and how long you stay. From this they work out what will probably interest you.
20355.m: What I watch affects what is suggested to me.

20356.q: What is it called when algorithms mainly show you content that matches your own opinion?
20356.e: The term filter bubble became well known in 2011 through Eli Pariser. Other points of view are shown less often.
20356.m: In a filter bubble, I mainly see what matches my opinion.

20357.q: What do the algorithms of many social networks mainly want to achieve?
a: That you stay on the platform as long as possible
That you put your phone away
That you only read the news
20357.e: The longer you stay, the more adverts you see. That is how platforms make their money.
20357.m: Platforms want me to stay as long as possible.

20358.q: What does the abbreviation AI stand for?
20358.e: Artificial intelligence means computer programs that learn from data and solve tasks that would otherwise need human thinking.

20359.q: What is a space online where like-minded people reinforce each other's opinions called?
20359.e: In an echo chamber, you mainly hear the echo of your own opinion. Other views hardly appear.
20359.m: In an echo chamber, I hear almost only my own opinion.

20360.q: How can you influence the suggestions of a recommendation algorithm?
a: By liking, searching and hiding things deliberately
20360.e: The algorithm learns from every action. If you deliberately look for other content or choose “not interested”, the suggestions change.
20360.m: I can influence the suggestions with my clicks.

a: All the traces you leave on the internet
A photo of your own foot
The size of the hard drive
20361.e: Your digital footprint includes posts, comments, photos, searches and data that websites collect about us.
20361.m: Everything I do online leaves traces.

20362.q: What does a browser's incognito mode prevent?
a: Your history being saved on your own device
20362.e: In private mode, history and cookies are deleted after closing. But providers and websites can still see what you do.
20362.m: Incognito mode does not make me invisible on the internet.

20363.q: Which information can be stored in the metadata of a phone photo?
20363.e: Photos often contain so-called EXIF data with the date, camera model and GPS location. When sharing, this can give away where you live.
20363.m: Photos can give away where they were taken.

20364.q: What does the saying “The internet never forgets” mean?
a: Something once published can hardly be deleted completely
The internet does not store data
20364.e: Posts can be copied, shared and archived. Even if you delete them, they may still exist somewhere else.
20364.m: What I post once can stay online forever.

20365.q: What is the right to ask search engines to remove certain links about yourself called?
20365.e: The European Court of Justice recognised this right in 2014 in a ruling against Google. It applies under certain conditions in the EU.
20365.m: Under certain conditions, you can have search results about yourself removed.

20366.q: Why can future employers offering apprenticeships see applicants' digital footprints?
a: Because public posts can be found with search engines
Because the school passes on all data
20366.e: Many companies search for applicants' names on the internet. Public photos and comments can leave an impression.
20366.m: I think about what I show about myself in public.

20367.q: Which setting stops apps from constantly recording where you are?
20367.e: In the settings you can decide for each app whether and when it may use your location. That way you leave fewer traces.
20367.m: I only share my location when it is necessary.

20368.q: What is phishing by text message called?
20368.e: Smishing combines SMS and phishing. It is often about supposed parcel deliveries or bank problems.
20368.m: Fraudsters can fish for data by text message too.

20369.q: What is phishing by phone call called?
20369.e: Vishing comes from “voice phishing”. On the phone, fraudsters pretend to be a bank or the police, for example.
20369.m: I do not give passwords or codes on the phone.

20370.q: What does a genuine bank never ask for by email?
a: An answer to a customer survey
20370.e: Banks never ask their customers for passwords or codes by email or text message. Such messages are almost always phishing.
20370.m: I never give out passwords by email.

20371.q: How can you often recognise a phishing email?
a: By time pressure and a false sender address
By a correct greeting with your name
By a logo in the footer alone
20371.e: Typical signs are threats like “Your account will be blocked”, mistakes in the text and sender addresses that do not match the company.
20371.m: If an email puts me under time pressure, I get suspicious.

20372.q: What is the federal office in Switzerland where you can report phishing and cyberattacks called?
20372.e: The Federal Office for Cyber Security (NCSC) has existed since 2024. It receives reports of cyber incidents and warns about new scams.
20372.m: I can report phishing to the Federal Office for Cyber Security.

20373.q: What should you do before clicking on a link in a suspicious email?
a: Hover the mouse over it and check the real address
20373.e: When you hover over it, the program shows the real target address. If it does not match the company, the link is fake.
20373.m: I check a link's address before I click.

a: Targeted phishing aimed at a particular person
Phishing with adverts for fishing gear
20374.e: In spear phishing, fraudsters tailor the message exactly to one person, for example with their name and real details. That makes it hard to recognise.
20374.m: Targeted scam messages can look very real.

a: A fake online shop that delivers nothing after payment
20375.e: Fake shops lure people with very low prices and demand payment in advance. The goods never arrive.
20375.m: If an offer is too good to be true, it is often a scam.

20376.q: What is a sign of a fake shop?
a: No legal notice and payment in advance only
20376.e: Genuine shops have a legal notice with an address and offer safe ways to pay. If both are missing, be careful.
20376.m: An online shop without a legal notice is suspicious.

a: A scam where feelings are faked to get money
A love film on the internet
A dating app for older people
20377.e: Fraudsters build up a romantic relationship online and then ask for money, for example for a supposed emergency.
20377.m: If someone only knows me online and wants money, that is suspicious.

20378.q: What is typical of an advance-fee scam?
a: You are asked to pay money first to get more later
You get a bill straight away
You have to sign a contract
20378.e: Fraudsters promise a prize or an inheritance but ask for fees first. The promised amount never comes.
20378.m: If you have to pay first to get a prize, you are being cheated.

20379.q: What should you do if a so-called support worker calls and wants remote access to your computer?
a: Hang up and not allow access
20379.e: In support scams, criminals pretend to work for well-known companies. With remote access they steal data or money.
20379.m: I do not give strangers access to my computer.

20380.q: Someone on the internet threatens to publish something embarrassing about you if you do not pay. What do you do?
a: Not pay, keep evidence and get help
20380.e: People who pay are often blackmailed again. It is better to take screenshots, stop contact and get help from adults, from the number 147 or from the police.
20380.m: If I am blackmailed, I do not pay and get help straight away.

a: A login with a password and a second proof
20381.e: As well as the password, you need a second factor, such as a code from an app or by text message. This protects accounts even if the password is stolen.
20381.m: A second factor gives my account extra protection.

20382.q: What is a message saying “You have won a new phone, click here” most likely to be?
a: A system message from the phone
20382.e: Promises of prizes without entering a competition are a classic trick. They lead to sites that grab data or money.

20383.q: How long is a work such as a book or a song protected by copyright in Switzerland?
a: Until 70 years after the creator's death
Until 25 years after the creator's death
20383.e: The Copyright Act protects works until 70 years after the death of the creator. After that they are in the public domain.
20383.m: Works are protected until 70 years after the creator's death.

20384.q: Can you simply copy a computer game you bought and sell the copies on the internet?
a: Yes, if it is more than a year old
Yes, if you lower the price
20384.e: Computer programs and games are protected by copyright. Anyone who copies and passes them on or sells them breaks the makers' rights.
20384.m: I may not copy and sell games I have bought.

20385.q: Who holds the copyright to a photo you took yourself?
a: The platform where it is shown
20385.e: Copyright belongs automatically to the person who creates a work. No registration is needed.
20385.m: Whoever creates a work holds the copyright to it.

20386.q: In Switzerland, what is the case when uploading copyrighted music without permission?
a: It is only allowed on Sundays
It is allowed if you share it
20386.e: Downloading music and films for your own use is allowed, but offering and uploading them without permission is not.
20386.m: I may not simply offer other people's music online.

a: Permissions with which creators allow use under conditions
20387.e: With Creative Commons, creators can decide how others may use their work, for example only with credit or not for commercial purposes.
20387.m: Creative Commons licences allow use under certain conditions.

20388.q: What does “BY” mean in a Creative Commons licence?
a: The creator's name must be given
The work is only for authorities
20388.e: BY requires attribution. Anyone who uses the work must say who it comes from.
20388.m: With CC BY, I always name the creator.

20389.q: What must you remember when quoting from someone else's text?
20389.e: Quotations are allowed if they serve to explain something and are marked as quotations. The source must be named.
20389.m: When I quote, I always give the source.

a: A work is no longer protected by copyright
A work belongs to the municipality
A work may only be read
20390.e: Once the protection period is over, anyone may use a work freely, for example Mozart's music.
20390.m: Anyone may use works in the public domain freely.

20391.q: What does the right to your own image mean?
a: You can basically decide yourself whether photos of you are published
You may use all photos on the internet
You must pay for every photo
20391.e: The right to your own image is part of the protection of personal rights. Anyone who wants to publish a photo of a recognisable person usually needs their consent.
20391.m: Before I post a photo of someone, I ask for permission.

20392.q: In which Swiss law is the protection of personal rights, which includes the right to your own image, laid down?
20392.e: Article 28 of the Civil Code protects personal rights against unlawful violation. The right to your own image is derived from it.
20392.m: The Civil Code protects my personal rights.

20393.q: What should you do before putting a class group photo online?
a: Make the photo black and white
Nothing, group photos are always allowed
20393.e: Every recognisable person has the right to their own image. That is why you need everyone's consent, and for children their parents' too.
20393.m: For a group photo, I ask everyone who is in it.

20394.q: What can you demand if a photo of you was published without permission?
20394.e: If the right to your own image is violated, you can demand its removal and contact the platform or, if necessary, a court.
20394.m: I can have photos of me that were posted without permission deleted.

20395.q: For children under 14, who usually also has to agree before a photo is published?
20395.e: Younger children often cannot yet judge the consequences of a photo being published. That is why their parents help decide.
20395.m: For younger children, parents help decide about photos.

20396.q: When is the consent of the person in a photo usually not needed to publish it?
a: When they only appear in the background of a large crowd
When the photo is black and white
When they are looking at the camera
When the photo was taken in your own garden
20396.e: If a person is only in a picture by chance and in the background, for example in a crowd at a festival, their personal rights are usually not violated. If they are the focus, their consent is usually needed.
20396.m: Anyone who is the focus of a photo usually has to be asked.

20397.q: Can you secretly film people at a swimming pool and share the video?
a: No, that violates their personal rights
Yes, if the video is short
Yes, if you only send it to friends
20397.e: Secret recordings of people in private or intimate situations violate their personal rights and can be a criminal offence.

20398.q: What is meant by digital identity?
a: All the features by which you are recognised online
The serial number of your phone
20398.e: Digital identity includes usernames, profiles, passwords, photos and data linked to a person on the internet.
20398.m: My digital identity is made up of everything that makes me who I am online.

a: A long password with different characters
20399.e: Long passwords with letters, numbers and special characters are hard to guess. Personal details are easy to find out.
20399.m: A good password is long and hard to guess.

20400.q: Why should you not use the same password for all your accounts?
a: Because then a data leak puts all accounts at risk
Because it is against the law
20400.e: If a password is stolen, attackers often try it on lots of services. Different passwords limit the damage.
20400.m: I use a separate password for every account.

20401.q: What is a password manager for?
a: It stores lots of passwords securely encrypted
20401.e: A password manager remembers lots of strong passwords. You only need to remember one master password.
20401.m: A password manager helps me use many secure passwords.

20402.q: What is identity theft on the internet?
a: Someone uses another person's data to pretend to be them
20402.e: Criminals open accounts or order goods in the victim's name, for example. To do this they use stolen personal data.
20402.m: I protect my data so that nobody can pretend to be me.

20403.q: What did Swiss voters decide in September 2025 about the state e-ID?
a: They did not vote at all
20403.e: On 28 September 2025, the federal law on electronic identity was narrowly accepted with about 50.4 per cent voting yes. The e-ID is issued by the federal government, is voluntary and, according to the Federal Council, is due to start at the end of 2026.
20403.m: Switzerland is introducing a voluntary state e-ID.

a: An account with a false identity
A profile with lots of photos
20404.e: Fake profiles pretend to be someone else, often with stolen photos. They are used for scams, bullying or advertising.
20404.m: Not every profile belongs to the person it shows.

a: A graphic figure that represents a person online
A virus in an email attachment
20405.e: An avatar is a profile picture or game character. It can help you avoid showing your own face online.
20405.m: With an avatar I do not have to show my real face.
